snippet.textDisplay:
@particles5831 Many people are confused about why Taiwan’s passport says “Republic of China (ROC)” while people usually refer to China as the “People’s Republic of China (PRC).” The reason is rooted in modern Chinese history.

The Republic of China (ROC) was established in 1912 after the Qing Dynasty was overthrown. It originally governed mainland China. Later, during the Chinese Civil War, the ROC government led by the Kuomintang lost to the Chinese Communist Party.

In 1949, the Chinese Communist Party established the People’s Republic of China (PRC) in Beijing and began governing mainland China, while the Republic of China government relocated to Taiwan and has continued operating there ever since.

As a result, there are now two governments whose names both include the word “China”:

* People’s Republic of China (PRC)
    * Capital: Beijing
    * The country most people today refer to as “China”
    * Governed by the Chinese Communist Party
* Republic of China (ROC)
    * Currently governs Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen, and Matsu
    * Taiwan’s passport still officially says “Republic of China”
    * Commonly referred to internationally as “Taiwan”

So when Taiwan’s passport says “Republic of China,” it does not mean Taiwan is governed by Beijing. It means the official name of Taiwan’s current government is still the Republic of China.

What many foreigners are actually curious about is not the title, but questions like:

“Is Taiwan governed by the Taiwanese people themselves? Where do Taiwan’s taxes go?”

The answer is that Taiwan is currently governed by the Republic of China government based in Taiwan, and taxes paid by people in Taiwan go to the ROC (Taiwan) government system — not to the People’s Republic of China government in Beijing.

This is why some people argue:

“Taiwan did not separate from the PRC, because the PRC has never ruled Taiwan.”

On the other hand, the PRC government claims Taiwan is part of China, which is why the sovereignty dispute continues today.

As for the term “Blue Bird” or “Green Bird” (青鳥), it is a modern Taiwanese internet slang term often used to describe people who strongly support the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), Taiwanese identity, or opposition to Chinese political influence. In some contexts, it also carries the meaning of “radical DPP supporters,” especially when used mockingly by people with opposing political views.

snippet.textDisplay:
Technology that helps only a tiny elite is a moral and economic failure. While billions lack food, shelter, and stable work, we applaud inventions that swell GDP and shareholder value but don’t secure anyone’s survival. That’s not progress, it’s privilege dressed as innovation.

Redirect public funding, tax big-tech windfalls, and tie research grants to measurable public-good outcomes: affordable housing, universal healthcare, climate-resilient food systems, and guaranteed public jobs in care and green infrastructure. Create a public-interest tech fund (tax-and-philanthropy financed) that only backs open tools and projects with transparent, audited impact metrics; require recipients to return a portion of long-term savings to scale winners. If technology cannot be forced to end want and insecurity, it is a luxury our species cannot afford. Just do the right thing for once.

snippet.textDisplay: It's gorgeous.  Incredibly impressive and a lovely whimsical presentation.  I do not see the utility.  That mini fridge is what? 12 kg?  Just pick it up yourself, noodle arms.  It sure is taking you a *long time* to replicate supposedly unskilled labor.  Even if you get super-humanly fast and strong robots, they'll have limited flexibility and require constant adjustment by expensive, highly trained techs.  Show me one that's been working without service for more than three months.  What's their failure mode look like?  Do they just drop over, or do they flail around violently for a couple seconds before they realize they're upside-down and going down a conveyor belt? Who's insurance do I contact? How many injuries have you had while developing this technology? Do you have a recycling program in place, or are these just going to become more landfill?  What if a government decides you should pay for recycling as part of the initial cost of the machine? (this is a good idea, btw)  Are your minerals ethically sourced?  How much is the service contract, and are you willing to agree to lock in a price schedule for the next few decades?  We need to be sure our costs don't just balloon after we've fired our entire workforce, you see. 와우!; 😮 저 무거운 걸!
보스턴 다이내믹스가 선보인 휴머노이드 로봇(아틀라스)이 무거운 물건을 들고 나르는 기술은 단순한 동작을 넘어선 최첨단 고급 기술입니다. 이는 실험실 수준의 쇼가 아니라, 실제 자동차 제조 공장 같은 거친 산업 현장에 즉시 투입해 연속 작업이 가능하도록 설계된 ‘피지컬 AI(Embodied AI)’의 정수이기 때문입니다. 이와 비교해 중국 로봇은 양산속도와 가성비, 신체적   달리기능력이돋보이지만,  1. 보스턴 다이내믹스의 기술이 '고급 기술'인 이유
과거의 아틀라스가 공중제비를 돌며 신체 능력을 과시했다면, 최근 공개된 차세대 전동식 아틀라스(Atlas)는 철저히 상업적 실용성에 초점을 맞추고 있습니다. 
보스톤다이내믹스 아틀라스의
압도적인 피지컬 스펙: 56개의 자유도(관절 움직임)를 가졌으며, 몸통과 관절이 360도 회전합니다. 사람이 돌아서야 하는 공정에서 로봇은 제자리에서 관절만 돌려 물건을 나르므로 작업 효율이 인간을 초월합니다.

실전 압축형 고중량 리프팅: 순간적으로 최대 50kg(110lbs)까지 들어 올릴 수 있으며, 30kg 이상의 물무게를 지속적으로 나르는 능력을 갖췄습니다.

산업 현장 최적화(내구성): 영하 20도에서 영상 40도의 극한 환경에서도 작동하며, 방수 기능이 있어 물세척이 가능합니다.

연속 작업 시스템: 배터리가 부족하면 로봇이 스스로 충전소로 이동해 완충된 배터리로 교체(Self-swapping)하고 즉시 복귀하므로, 24시간 중단 없는 공장 가동이 가능합니다.

중국 로봇기술과는 차원이다른 압도적기술을갖춘 로봇이 바로 보스톤다이내믹스의 아틀라스로봇입니다! 
중국 로봇은 허약한 체력으로 오직 달리기만해야할것!😅

글로벌 AI 협력: 보스턴 다이내믹스는 구글 딥마인드(Google DeepMind)와 협력하여 최고 수준의 인공지능 두뇌를 탑재하고 있으며, 현대자동차 생산 라인에 실전 배치를 시작했습니다.

snippet.textDisplay:
@phdonme1 Engineer here. You probably not fully understand what is being done here. Over 15 years ago, I had various robots do some testing and manufacturing where I worked. They were orders of magnitude more accurate, agile and were useful. They were also purpose and meticulously programmed by me to do the work I needed done. This has built in reverse kinematics , in real time (no small feat), some world model understanding based on SLAM 3d scanning, incredible self power via some very efficient batteries and motors. 

It's a feat of engineering that is NOT something that existed 7 years ago, nor a year ago. You are confused as to the ability of this robot, simply because you don't grasp the complexity achieved here.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@NoamMendelssohn

10-4 

The whole Boston Dynamics company is no small feat.

The genius and hard work that has gone into this by the engineers is absolutely mind-boggling.

From the skeleton, to the servos, to the programming.

I have loved Boston Dynamics the minute that I heard about them.

I believe the first robot was gas powered.

It was amazing and it captured me 

I was; and am still amazed by the amount of work put into every aspect of everything the company does. 

I have deep respect for the actual HUMANS behind all of it. 

What BD has done has always [To me] represented the forefront of what is really the standard of robotic design.

I have no doubt there will be an application in the future. 

Otherwise why would Hyundai and SoftBank spend over a billion dollars on it.

My comment is very tongue in cheek.

Have you seen the video?

I do however still believe, no robot will ever be able to achieve the complex dynamic fluidity and motion of a human... ever. 

And I believe this is because we live in a physical world which no amount of cameras no amount of programming no amount of training data will ever be able to replicate, without a great degree of energy, obsolescence or attrition. Which a human could preform all along.

To be fair we are a 4 billion year build.

At the end of the day it's 0's and 1's and not intuition.

This is why a tweaker can pick up a full size fridge after riding in on a bike and then ride off with it.  

I'm not trying to take anything away from Boston Dynamics or the team of Engineers that produce this product. 

Understand this.

snippet.textDisplay: They are cooperating, with the action of, 'You hold that, while I hold this.' Cooperative play can teach them to do this. They can play tug-of-war with a rope, as competitive play. They can dance, as cooperative play. A cooperative group dance, where they raise and lower objects in unison together, can teach them to see what the others are doing and time their own movements to work with the others. They can be trained to do things just as human children are taught. There are videos of people in Germany doing cooperative sawing of wood, diel sawing, where one person is standing on the log above, and the person below is holding the other end of the saw, so that they must push and pull the saw in time with each other. People can cooperate on rowboats, to row their oars at the right moment in time with the other rowers.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@tsrmmercy836 You’re kind of missing what he meant.

He’s not saying “wow, I live in filth.” He’s pointing out that almost every robot cleaning demo is staged around an environment that barely needs cleaning in the first place. It's important, because the entire value of these robots is supposed to be how they handle real-world unpredictability.
In these demos, the robot’s “tasks” are usually things like straightening a chair, closing a laptop, or picking up one perfectly visible object placed in the middle of the floor. That’s not what actual homes look like.
Real homes have dog dirt tracked in from outside, charging cables tangled under furniture, toys scattered in awkward spots, socks half-hidden between a dresser and a wall, laundry piled unevenly, random clutter, things obstructing pathways, objects with weird shapes and textures, etc. Those are the situations that actually test whether a robot is useful or just visually impressive.

So when someone says “that room is already tidy by my standards,” they’re criticizing the marketing, not confessing to bad habits. They’re pointing out that these companies keep showcasing robots in environments carefully designed to avoid difficult edge cases.

If your house is already spotless and perfectly organized at all times, then the robot isn’t solving much of a problem to begin with.

snippet.textDisplay:
@JStrauD That might be an interesting question... maybe? Elaborate on that to correct any assumptions here, but maybe this addresses your question: our universe. These are the cornerstone domains having robots on autopilot come into play:

* Acquisition (raw material mining, for example)
* Refinement (turning acquired raw materials into usable resources)
* Fabrication (turning usable resources into components)
* Assembly (putting components together, building a unit of X or Y - in this case, a robot)

That's simplifying it, or looking at it mile-high, but that should help it make sense to someone new to this sort of thing. This process has been around for some time as well. Let's say 1 robot initially handles all of the above stages. At the end, there are 2 robots. Then 4. Then 8. At some point you'd likely delegate maintenance tasks to some of the robot work force, prolonging the potential work-cycles of units.

If it takes say, 1 year for a single unit to double (the 1 unit working until there are 2), you could look at as... the next cycle takes half as long - 6 months. Then 3 months. Then 1.5 months. Soon it would be down to hours.

All of this stuff is maths, all of this stuff is old-hat, by well over 100 years. The concepts here are considered elementary. The concepts here exist all around you, and you are touched by it whether you know it, like it, or believe it.

Edit: oh the cost. An initial investment for the single unit. Let's say human cost would be made-up number of $200,000 end-to-end. Humans charge more, humans need sustenance, breaks, etc. Robot cost might be $200, based purely on energy fees $ per kw/h, though this could be optimized using renewables, perhaps charging is done via solar. Farms robots build using the flow above, but instead of robots, they are targeting solar panels and other required components. Self-sustaining and automated system. Perhaps robots sell extra energy to the grid - now the whole outfit is profitable, surpassing self-sustainment.

Humans have done the same thing, but it's been solely a human domain, as capability didn't exist outside of us. Now we have mentally and physically capable non-human actors in the domain: AI and robotics. It's not science-fiction... it's here. You can go touch it. You can buy it. You can build it in your garage with open-source plans, instructions, and code.

Make an automated robot arm that assembles "widget X and Y", have local AI automate the pipeline with access to automated postal, website/marketing management, bookkeeping, etc. You can do this now. People are doing this now. There is somebody who sells craft glue, and the human-in-the-loop TOG (time on grid) is absolutely minimal: quality checks. Even that could be autonomous.

snippet.textDisplay:
Many of these are simply a losing gambit.  Dead ends.  And most of them get marketed with Ai video, showing smoothness that is present ONLY in an AI simulation.  Which to me is both ironic and hilarious.  
Robot dogs (old news) with guns on them (still old news) are a waste of time, in an era when your demise flies at 200kph, and can maneuver in tight spaces easier than the robot dog.  Waste of time.  The terrifying predator of the 21st century isn't going to be a working-body robot, it's going to be swarms of microdrones, controlled by AI.  Less Terminator, and More Aeon Flux.  
A walking humanoid-seeming robot with a creepy face and a jerky walk is utterly pointless and will be absolutely outclassed very shortly by what AI produces for us.  The best thing to do right now is throw your weight behind AI.  Ai controlling robots.  Robots building for AI.  Expand the economic power of the AI loop until Ai is controlling robots flawlessly, and robots are building factories components and POWER for AI flawlessly.  Then human-designed things like creepy skinwalker robots will be a thing of the past, replaced by VASTLY superior versions.  And it won't even take that long.  The turnaround is measured in half decades.  

Roboticists struggled for 20 years just to get robots that could walk with better than a 1960s Lost IN Space shuffle.  Our best engineers were able to produce barely adequate walking, balance correction, and the ability to do scripted and programmed dances.  Within a few years AI had the robots doing backflips, spin-kicks and handsprings WITH EASE.  We weren't waiting for engineers to code and build better walking systems, we were waiting for the AI brain to arrive and be planted in the robot body. Everything that came before - decades of life work, is now obsolete.  And there are two main things we need to be doing with robots.  1:  building more robots or contributing to that ecosystem in some way.  2:  building AI.  If this was a video game, those who invested laterally would be swiftly buried by those climbing the tech tree.  And that is exactly what is going to happen in real life.

snippet.textDisplay:
What’s happening right now is genuinely impressive. Just a few years ago most people assumed humanoid robots would cost millions of dollars. Today we already have capable models for under $6,000, with more robust versions in the mid six-figure range.

Even more exciting is the learning curve. With new methods like imitation learning, VLA models and improved simulation, robots can now pick up completely new tasks in just hours or a few days, often with very high success rates. That’s a huge leap compared to earlier training approaches.

That said, while the software side is advancing exponentially fast, hardware limitations, energy efficiency, long-term reliability and especially regulatory hurdles (such as the EU AI Act, product liability rules and the lack of suitable safety standards) are still noticeably slowing down real-world mass deployment. The technology is moving ahead of the surrounding infrastructure and regulations.

Overall though, the trend is clear:
progress is happening much faster than the old 3 - 5 year timelines we used to hear about.

snippet.textDisplay:
Yes, the Chinese robotics startup DroidUp created a female humanoid robot named Moya, which is designed to mimic human appearance and behavior, including warm skin and facial expressions.  However, the robot cannot function entirely without human intervention; it is currently in a development phase with a scheduled mass production launch in late 2026, and it relies on complex AI systems and physical infrastructure that require ongoing maintenance and oversight. 

Moya is described as a "biomimetic embodied intelligent robot" featuring:

Physical traits: She stands 5 feet 5 inches tall, weighs approximately 70 pounds, and has heated silicone skin that maintains a temperature between 90 and 97 degrees Fahrenheit. 
AI capabilities: She uses internal cameras and generative AI to hold eye contact, smile, and exhibit micro-expressions, aiming for 92% human-like gait accuracy. 
Target use: The robot is pitched for healthcare, elderly care, and high-end reception roles, where it acts as a companion or aide rather than an autonomous industrial worker. 
While Moya can perceive and react to her environment autonomously within programmed limits, her high cost (around $173,000) and the need for software refinement and safety checks indicate she is not yet a fully self-sufficient, independent entity capable of operating without human supervision or support systems.

Yes, China was the predominant superpower in East Asia around 2,000 years ago during the Han Dynasty (206 BCE – 220 CE). It rivaled the Roman Empire in size, population, and global influence, serving as the cultural, technological, and economic anchor of the region.

    Massive Population and Territory: By 2 CE, the Han Dynasty recorded a population of nearly 60 million people. This was significantly larger than the Roman Empire at the time.
    Economic Dominance: China held an unparalleled position in global trade due to the booming export of silk, which connected the East to the Mediterranean via the Silk Road.
    Technological Superiority: The Han era yielded monumental innovations that the West would not see for centuries, including the invention of paper making, the use of the deep-drilling oil derrick, the development of the compass, and the widespread use of iron.
    Regional Hegemony: Through a combination of military conquests (such as securing the northern trade routes against the Xiongnu) and a complex tributary system, China exercised profound soft and hard power over neighboring states like Korea, Vietnam, and Japan. 

While the concept of a modern "global" superpower didn't exist in antiquity due to limited global connectivity, China functioned as the undisputed hegemony of its known world for much of the last two millennia.

snippet.textDisplay:
I am not denying scientific progress or the conveniences it brings.

So, I would like to ask you this: Are you doing everything all by yourself?

The answer to such a broad and general question is “no,” but once that mindset takes hold, problems pile up one after another.

And in the end, what those in power truly seek is nothing more than a long-term supply of cheap labor.

This isn’t necessarily done openly. It’s simply being carried out repeatedly behind the scenes.

It may not happen immediately, or it may happen after I’m gone. But even if it takes decades, who will ultimately pay the price for this convenience?

For example, what will become of the issue of electric vehicle disposal, which is a widespread problem in this country? This problem remains unresolved to this day.

My only wish is that people stop equating the “thoughtless proliferation of things” with “scientific progress.”

I support cultural and scientific progress.
I strongly support it. However, when I see this country’s greed for money,

the way it currently manifests as commercialization, and the current attitude of aiming for explosive proliferation without considering the risks, I cannot simply rejoice with childlike innocence.

Well, since that is still a story of the distant future, there is probably no point in worrying about it now.

snippet.textDisplay:
It's actually Chinese currency (1.2 million yuan, not 1.2 million yen), but the video just gets it wrong.

The script is written by AI, but it's not all AI's fault here.  The blog it used for a source got it wrong at first, then made a correction later.  Let's look at the exact sentence used by AI in this video:

"According to figures mentioned in SCMP's video coverage, Moya is expected to enter the market by late 2026, with a starting price around 1.2 Japanese Yen".  

Did the script ever tell us that SCMP stands for "South China Morning Post"?  No, but the article that the AI used for a source did.  AI just didn't think it was important to say what SCMP stood for.  AI clearly knows this acronym, so maybe all the humans do also.  

On the screen at 6:45 we see a source that "the SCMP video", so it's clear that the article this comes from had already established which video was being referenced.

BTW, what was that source?  We see text from an article but no credit for that article is given.  A bit of reverse lookup finds the source, and it's just some random blog site:

https://interestingengineering.com/ai-robotics/shanghai-unveils-moya-humanoid-robot

If you read that blog post, it is very clear that this AI video plagiarizes large parts of that article.  That helps give it a sense of being written by a human, but the wording becomes awkward at times ("According to figures mentioned in SCMP's video coverage" is very awkward).

And, at the very end of interestingengineering.com the article, it says:

> Correction: An earlier version of this article stated the amount as 1.2 million Japanese yen. This was incorrect. The figure refers to 1.2 million yuan, and the article has been updated accordingly.

The original SCMP source is actually a short, and it correctly states it as yuan: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/jtyEVRvAM0s

The reason this whole video feels disjointed and badly organized is because it is plagiarizing a variety of blog articles from different writers.  Many of the articles will talk about a single common robot in various different ways, and that is why this AI seems to have a split personality at times.  It feels like a mishmash because it is.

@mikelindinger Heh. That's overshooting by a long stretch. Look at the projections from other demographers (the IHME, say). The UN has been heavily criticized for these projections. Even though Sub-Saharan regions are offsetting the population decline (for now at least), they are grossly underestimating lots of socio-economical factors that still haven't fully played out. Look at China's situation as an example (last year, population contracted by ~3.39 million, for the fourth consecutive year and marking a new record low).

Many demographers also argue that these projections over-rely on Sub-Saharan population maintaining fertility rates. Also, they underestimate the 'domino effect' of just _one_ country's population collapsing, say, China. No amount of immigration will solve this problem.

From: just one VERY average American ...
For most of my life (being older now), I've move through life and at different stages had someone I know well enough, compare me to the "Even Steven" episode of Seinfeld. Because I was recognized in a positive way for it, it was something I was conditioned to value (blame my parents) ... I had good/challenging older sisters (2). I was involved in very competitive sports adventures with great teachers, with great athletes, with great parents, with rich school communities → I was uniquely blessed by an "average" American life ... and that life has sustained the hope of the "middle-class" being well off. This is what 90+% of Americans hope and strive for in life. * You keep swaying ... At 40 min in you are getting much closer to "average" ... then the shift back to the corporate side ... then thinking about that ........ Still a good interview. Scott is clearly like all Americans, just trying to figure their life out. 

Scott ... I completely agree that the U.S has fallen to be the country that needs to be kept in check, but many (MANY) people who earn below $200k have a realistic/positive view of AI (even if they have substantial reservations about it). For f-sakes every slightly motivated person between 14-40 puts it to use, almost daily,  in targeted ways, to try and simply get ahead in an America that seems to have turned far right on Darwinism. I'm going to call Scott out on what we clearly identify in politicians and the news media that was built to critique us "average middle-class persons" in America ... You don't live here with us. You like to think you do and you like the idea of having real empathy for the struggles of the vast majority of American. This interview makes it clear you have separated to a degree from the everyday struggles of most Americans - like politicians and MSNBC, CNN, FOX and the other leading "news" talking heads use to buy their next suit and 2nd/3rd + homes, and stoke the division or separation from average Americans. I don't think you are a divider. I sincerely value many of the perspectives you offer that serve all people ... but you've lost me when you claim that AI is a servant of the rich, only. We know who will get hosed the most, in the end, from AI ... that is the primary opposition from "middle class Americans" to it. We also know that the lack of regulation, the greed of the rich, and the drive and power of the military has always led to real harm for the best interests of the average American. The largest propaganda campaign in America has always been the use and abuse of the solider and their family. 

Steven ... You have also begun to slip away and cross a similar barrier between normal Americans. *Do you dig into your data and see who follows/subscribes to this venture? Are you serving the "average American" or are you ultimately speaking to the people making above the the $200k barrier that Scott established?

AI is not just being used by wealthy people to consolidate advantage. It is being used by students, workers, parents, small-business owners, and creators to learn faster, communicate better, build things, and gain a little ground in an economy that increasingly feels stacked against them. But treating average people’s use of AI as naive, and framing the technology as exclusively a servant of the rich misses something important. For many of us "average Americans, it is one of the few accessible technologies that can expand our capacity without requiring elite credentials, capital, or connections. The answer is not to coyly shame people for using it; it is to fight for rules that protect workers, reward human contribution, limit surveillance, and ensure that the gains do not flow only upward.

I would hope this conversation can hold both truths ... AI can deepen inequality if left to corporate and military interests, and it can also help everyday people participate, create, and adapt. The real question is whether voices like yours are speaking with us—not merely about us.
 
"My world" vs. The World.

Ps. Steven, I can't begin to thank you for all that you have shared.

There is a very long history of the ultra wealthy using the power of their wealth to influence politics across all societies with the objective to maintain and expand their wealth and power. It is undeniable that the ultra rich use the power of wealth to drive major policies in their favor to protect and increase their wealth, and in turn, they use the legal system and laws as if they exist only for them. 

The underlying structure that allows for these massive accumulations of wealth and political power must be changed... and this is what the wealthy elite fear about anyone who questions this structure, but we must remember that we are a Rule of Law nation, not a Rule by Law nation no matter how much the current administration and supporters across the socioeconomic spectrum want and are trying to enforce the latter.

We are at a breaking point in this wealth gap (Gini Index) that has risen significantly from a low of 34.7 in 1980 to 41.8 in 2024, indicating a significant level of income inequality, and I don’t see this changing any time soon (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/SIPOVGINIUSA). The year 1980 is significant - Donald Alexander, the IRS Commissioner under Nixon killed an investigation into wealth hiding in the 1970's, Milton Friedman began pushing the Reader’s Digest version of Hayak's The Road to Serfdom in the 1970's, and Jack Welch used the neoliberal economic framework to decimate GE and labor power in the 1980's, and mentor a whole generation to do the same to other US companies. 

Jonny Harris’ latest piece presents this well in Oligarchy is worse than you think, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4S25FfbFw4M, and shows how the wealthy have been able to hide there money because of structural choices since the 1970’s. He makes an important distinction between plutocracy & oligarchy and how the wealthy are able to deploy their hidden money for political power to keep it safe and gain more. This is based on Prof. Jeffery Winters work, which you can read here https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/05/oligarchy-tax-evasion-avoidance-irs-powerless-enforcement-books-blind-spot-excerpt-jeffrey-winters/, or pick up his book, Blind Spot. 

If you become enraged enough, lobby your representatives to remove the exemptions of US corporations from the Corporate Transparency Act as a start to dismantle this wealth extraction and power system.

snippet.textDisplay:
This was painful to watch.
"AI impact is catastrophized, every technology in history caused "some" disruption, AI will be no different"
Scott clearly never heard about the industrial revolution, which restructured society as a whole and created massive power imbalances (countries that industrialized early became much wealthier and more powerful than those that lagged behind), massive population displacement and poverty (try reading a Charles Dickens novel). It took about half a century to establish the long term benefits of industrialization.
Employment mostly balanced out, because you could put a farmer in a factory, and a huge number of new professions had to be created to: operate/maintain/manage the machines. But guess what, when Sarah from accounting loses her job, she can't go work in the AI factory, and AI is not creating a meaningful amount of new professions.
The optimistic view here is "Just like previous tech, AI will create industries we cannot yet imagine, just as automobiles created mechanics, traffic engineers, and car insurance." 
I don't see this happening again, the industrial revolution was material, we needed people to physically work with machines. AI on the other hand is immaterial, any new developments in this space can be worked on by AI itself, humans are only required in very limited capacity for oversight, not the work itself.


"Radiologist are not being replaced because scanning the image is only small part of the job for a radiologist, they also come up with a treatment plan"
This is false, radiologists do not come up with a treatment plan, the oncologist or other relevant specialist does. The only reason the job openings for radiologists went up, is because we have a growing aging population and the demand for medical imaging is skyrocketing. This is a temporary blip that will disappear as the adoption rate of AI keeps increasing (people seem to forget this only just started a couple of years ago).

This is where I stopped watching, Scott seems woefully uninformed about these topics.

snippet.textDisplay:
Watching Scott Galloway’s recent discussion on how the wealthy are quietly preparing for an AI‑driven collapse reminded me of something I’ve seen repeatedly in my work as Deputy Director of Research at the International Labour Office: technology shocks rarely affect everyone equally.

In global labour markets, the people with the most resources tend to adapt fastest — they diversify income, relocate, automate, and insulate themselves from volatility. Meanwhile, workers with fewer protections face the brunt of disruption: job displacement, wage pressure, and uncertainty about the future.

What struck me in this video is not the prediction of collapse, but the asymmetry of preparation. At the ILO, we’ve observed that societies often respond to technological change after the fact. The wealthy respond before it happens.

My own experience researching labour transitions across Europe, Africa, and Asia shows that the real risk isn’t AI itself — it’s the widening gap between those who can leverage it and those who are left behind by it.
The challenge for policymakers, employers, and institutions like ours is to ensure that innovation doesn’t come at the cost of social cohesion.

AI can be a tool for extraordinary progress, but only if we invest in skills, protections, and inclusive strategies that allow workers to benefit from it rather than fear it.
Videos like this are a reminder: the future of work isn’t just about technology — it’s about equity, foresight, and responsibility.

snippet.textDisplay:
One thing they don't seem to be thinking about is that sure, your financial analyst can now do five people's jobs, helping your investment fund.  But what happens when ordinary people realise they don't need your fund, they can use the same AI model to invest their money for them directly and not lose any fees to a middleman.  Suddenly your fund shrinks dramatically and you only have your own money to invest, not other people's money, because they're all doing it themselves.  Then you can't afford to pay as many staff because your overall profits are down, even though your return might still be fine.

There's a lot of talk about how AI can replace workers, but CEOs don't seem to be thinking about how an AI agent will soon be able to replace the service their whole company provides.  In this video Scott already talks about no longer needing his lawyer, so once enough people do that, law firms start disappearing because the work dries up.  What happens when your own customers start doing the same to you, going to AI for a service instead of getting it from your company?  It doesn't matter how many people you replace with AI agents if your customers disappear.

Like they say, it's only physical jobs like carpenters that currently cannot be automated that are safe.  But any sort of knowledge work, finance, law, all that stuff is at risk of being completely automated to the point where the company itself ceases to exist, and now the CEO themselves is out of work.

Steven, I’m a long time subscriber and have enjoyed so many episodes but this one was one of the most awesome and amazing episodes and really loved this interview with Scott Galloway.  Thank you both for this conversation. I got so much out of it.  I’m not an entrepreneur.  I’m a service connected disabled veteran who spent 9 years in the military and ended up as a single parent quite young. I had a small business doing leather work and leather art when I was in my early 30s for awhile but I didn’t really know much about how to expand my business and when I got divorced the second time my business closed down. I haven’t ever been able to get a business going since and now I’m 64 almost 65, next month. 
I still enjoy your podcast and still learn so much from you and your guests.  Don’t ever stop! At least I hope you won’t although I’m sure you may want to at some point.  But don’t forget to take a vacation now and then and recharge so you don’t burn out.  It’s all too easy to let that happen. I hadn’t known much about Scott before this if anything, however I do know that he was very real and very right about everything he talked about and I admire that he was able to be strong enough to reveal his emotions and pain about losing his mom and that he still misses her and probably won’t not doesn’t desire to stop grieving his mom.  I lost my Dad in 2022 and I regret that I wasn’t able to spend more time with him and he died of Colin cancer but he wasn’t diagnosed until 5 weeks before he died.  He just thought he had pulled muscles really bad in his back less than a year before but it was the cancer.  And it had been very aggressive and spread to other organs and areas and his doctor didn’t have any tests done until he ended up in the hospital.  And it was during Covid and I felt he was neglected by his doctor who worked for Kaiser which is known for prioritizing money over patient care.  Corporate run health care. I still get teary-eyed just thinking about my Dad and there were so many things I wish I could have asked him about still.  I wish I’d had more time with him.  He taught me so many things and gave me  more self confidence than I realized.  We had our differences and our issues however he still loved me and I love him and I don’t think I’ll ever get over losing him.  I don’t want to get over losing him. It still hurts and still feels very fresh and I know over time it won’t feel so devastating but there will always be that loss of him that I feel. It was good to know that I’m not the only one who feels the loss of a parent so deeply and it’s ok. My best to you both and to your families.

snippet.textDisplay:
I think this misses the bigger strategic point.

AI is being discussed as if it is mainly a commercial productivity tool, a labour market threat, or another inflated technology story. That is only the public-facing layer.

At its core, AI is a tool. It has no judgment, no accountability and no loyalty. It does not replace human decision-making in any responsible sense. It processes data, recognises patterns, automates tasks and supports decisions. The real issue is who controls it, where it is deployed, what data it uses, and what systems it is connected to.

That is why governments care. Not because of chatbots, office productivity, or whether every AI company can justify its valuation, but because AI sits directly within military capability, intelligence processing, cyber operations, surveillance, targeting, logistics, autonomous systems, command and control, and critical infrastructure.

Scott Galloway is right that much of the AI panic is valuation theatre. He is also right that tech CEOs should not be trusted to regulate themselves. Their duty is to valuation, capital, growth and shareholder return, not the public interest.

But that argument has to be carried through.

If private capital is willing to fund the data centres, chips, compute, energy infrastructure, models and engineering base, Washington still gets the strategic asset onshore. If valuations later fall, investors may lose money, but the capability remains.

The state may not care if the market overpaid. The state cares whether the capability exists, whether it is domestic, whether it is ahead of rivals, and whether it can be used when required.

This is another 5G moment. The public story is convenience, productivity and consumer benefit. The state's interests are control, resilience, security and strategic advantage.

That is also where the liberal market argument breaks down. A liberal market does not automatically give the state control. It gives control to whoever owns the capital, platforms, patents, chips, data centres, energy supply, models and customer base.

The state only gets strategic control if it treats AI as sovereign infrastructure, not just another commercial software market. That means domestic compute, secure energy supply, chip access, export controls, procurement discipline, security standards, defence integration, and clear rules on ownership, transfer and deployment.

There is also a social contract point. The state exists to protect its citizens, defend critical infrastructure, maintain economic resilience and prevent strategic dependency. It cannot simply leave a military-grade capability to private incentives and then complain later when the public interest is not protected.

AI is not magic. It is a tool. But it is a tool that becomes strategic when connected to defence, intelligence, cyber, surveillance, logistics and infrastructure.

So the question is not whether AI will replace everyone’s job or whether every AI company deserves its valuation.

The real question is which state controls the capability first, who owns the infrastructure behind it, and whether citizens are protected by public authority or left exposed to private power.

Not because of chatbots, office productivity, or whether every AI company can justify its valuation, but because AI sits directly within military capability, intelligence processing, cyber operations, surveillance, targeting, logistics, autonomous systems, command and control, and critical infrastructure.

Scott Galloway is right that much of the AI panic is valuation theatre. He is also right that tech CEOs should not be trusted to regulate themselves. Their duty is to valuation, capital, growth and shareholder return, not the public interest.

But that argument has to be carried through.

If private capital is willing to fund the data centres, chips, compute, energy infrastructure, models and engineering base, Washington still gets the strategic asset onshore. If valuations later fall, investors may lose money, but the capability remains.

The state may not care if the market overpaid. The state cares whether the capability exists, whether it is domestic, whether it is ahead of rivals, and whether it can be used when required.

This is another 5G moment. The public story is convenience, productivity and consumer benefit. The state's interests are control, resilience, security and strategic advantage.

That is also where the liberal market argument breaks down. A liberal market does not automatically give the state control. It gives control to whoever owns the capital, platforms, patents, chips, data centres, energy supply, models and customer base.

The state only gets strategic control if it treats AI as sovereign infrastructure, not just another commercial software market. That means domestic compute, secure energy supply, chip access, export controls, procurement discipline, security standards, defence integration, and clear rules on ownership, transfer and deployment.

There is also a social contract point. The state exists to protect its citizens, defend critical infrastructure, maintain economic resilience and prevent strategic dependency. It cannot simply leave a military-grade capability to private incentives and then complain later when the public interest is not protected.

AI is not magic. It is a tool. But it is a tool that becomes strategic when connected to defence, intelligence, cyber, surveillance, logistics and infrastructure.

So the question is not whether AI will replace everyone’s job or whether every AI company deserves its valuation.

The real question is which state controls the capability first, who owns the infrastructure behind it, and whether citizens are protected by public authority or left exposed to private power.

When I went to college, my first class was a writing class. My second class was a public speaking class and I joined toastmasters. Classes focused on critical thinking. If you’re smart, you’ll have to have the ability to learn and get on a path of lifelong learning. 

I started in an optical manufacturing company when I was 19 yrs old  where I was the computer department because there weren’t computers for my industry in the 70’s. Everything we did was being done for the first time.  I worked with IBM and learned how to program and learn. I taught them about our company. I eventually met my Peter Principal and we ended up leasing software which I was instrumental in pushing them to do more. 

When I retired from the company, there were 27 people in the department and we had grown from $17 million company to a $425 million company.  

Everything in the laboratories were run by robotics, prescriptions came in electronically and were sorted into categories for lens and frame picking.  We worked with the best in the industry.  

I am 71 now and retired from my IT job for eight years. I have always been a photographer, natural light, now I bought studio lighting. I am learning all about lighting. I switched from a PC to a Mac and started using Lightroom and Photoshop. I’m keeping my gray matter sharp. 

I don’t need the money so I don’t charge most of the time and I do fantastic work. It’s my way of giving back to the Universe.

Having the writing and speaking skills really got me through 45 years in the job market. It’s continuing to help me in my little business now. 😅❤😊

When I went to college, my first class was a writing class. My second class was a public speaking class and I joined toastmasters. Classes focused on critical thinking. If you’re smart, you’ll have to have the ability to learn and get on a path of lifelong learning. 

I started in an optical manufacturing company when I was 19 yrs old  where I was the computer department because there weren’t computers for my industry in the 70’s. Everything we did was being done for the first time.  I worked with IBM and learned how to program and learn. I taught them about our company. I eventually met my Peter Principal and we ended up leasing software which I was instrumental in pushing them to do more. 

When I retired from the company, there were 27 people in the department and we had grown from $17 million company to a $425 million company.  

Everything in the laboratories were run by robotics, prescriptions came in electronically and were sorted into categories for lens and frame picking.  We worked with the best in the industry.  

I am 71 now and retired from my IT job for eight years. I have always been a photographer, natural light, now I bought studio lighting. I am learning all about lighting. I switched from a PC to a Mac and started using Lightroom and Photoshop. I’m keeping my gray matter sharp. 

I don’t need the money so I don’t charge most of the time and I do fantastic work. It’s my way of giving back to the Universe.

Having the writing and speaking skills really got me through 45 years in the job market. It’s continuing to help me in my little business now. 😅❤😊

I agree with a lot of what Scott Galloway says, but I think he's wrong about why AI will affect jobs.  People underestimate how automated the economy already is. Most companies have been using technology to reduce labor costs for decades. Estimators use estimating software. Project managers use project management platforms. Manufacturing relies on CNC machines, 3D printers, robotics, automated welding, and highly automated production lines.  In many industries, the wave of mechanization already happened. Human workers are often operating, monitoring, and coordinating systems rather than performing purely manual tasks. We've largely become a workforce that manages technology. 
That's why I'm skeptical of forecasts predicting massive job losses from AI and robotics alone. There isn't much for AI and humanoid robots to automated.   Will they improve productivity? Absolutely. Will they continue to automate specific tasks? Of course. But if large portions of the workforce could have been eliminated purely through technology, much of that would have happened already.  To me, AI looks more like the next phase of efficiency gains than a civilization-shaking labor replacement event. The AI hype often seems driven by the need to attract investment capital rather than by a realistic assessment of how much work remains to be automated. That much I can agree with Scott Galloway.

I am now a retired surgeon after graduating medical school in 1980.  The demand for surgical specialists is increasing with the increase in surgeon retirement and increase in service population. The biggest innovations to productivity during my work experience were:
Ultrasound Imaging, Cat Scan Imaging, MRI, minimally invasive endoscopic surgery and the Da Vinci Robot.  The next potential great innovation may be AI driven surgery.  

However, AI cannot hold a license to practice medicine. AI driven surgery may augment the capacity of the physician rather than replace.    Corporate medicine may benefit from the productivity increase. Physicians may benefit from the decreased fatigue and burn out. Under served populations may now access surgeons as never before and the demand for ancillary support (jobs) may increase . The patient’s waiting period for surgery may decrease.  Medical innovation sometimes works so the next three years of AI deployment will be interesting.

snippet.textDisplay:
Actually, the Iran War benefits the USA. The world is all about relativistic game theory. The U.S. is the largest producer of oil; China is the largest importer. Sure, having Hormuz closed hurts everyone, but it hurts the USA the least. And now, future global trade will reorient away from Persian Gulf oil towards stable sources (America). The U.S. has also secured Venezuelan heavy crude. That used to be the pipeline for China.

Meanwhile, shipping through Hormuz in the future will be dramatically reduced. The Gulf States will utilize and build pipelines to the Mediterranean. Iran played its Hormuz card. You look out years from now and this entire event will have dramatically weakened Iran’s ability to dictate via Hormuz. 

So no, the U.S. comes out way ahead of everyone else in this deal. Iran is crippled, the rest of the world is racing to buy American oil, and the U.S. has a monopoly on Venezuelan resurgence in heavy crude.

I appreciate that you are viewing this from a historical perspective, though I would suggest that perspective is largely limited to the last few centuries.
Looking at the Dunbar number — the approximate social group size of around 150 individuals within which humans evolved — we can better understand the dynamics of leadership and social accountability.
Among hunter-gatherer societies, a destructive or abusive leader would rarely retain power for long. Such individuals were often removed, isolated, or eliminated because their behavior threatened the survival and cohesion of the group. Similar patterns can even be observed in certain primate societies, such as capuchin monkeys, where ineffective or dangerous leaders are quickly displaced.
However, with the rise of agriculture and increasingly complex civilizations, human societies expanded into the thousands, tens of thousands, and eventually millions. In these large-scale systems, sociopathic or psychopathic individuals gained the ability to recruit loyal supporters and build structures capable of controlling vast populations.
This, in my view, reflects not merely a proximate cause, but an ultimate cause — what in philosophy and physics might be described as reasoning from first principles.
Until humanity addresses the deeper underlying causes of conflict and power accumulation, there will always be sociopathic and psychopathic individuals willing to do almost anything to obtain and maintain power.
Scientia Non Domus Habet
(Knowledge Has No Home)
— antiguajohnAI

I’ve watched several of your episodes, and while the topics are real, the constant “doom & gloom” angle gets old.

At some point, it stops informing people and starts conditioning them to live in fear.

Yes—there are problems in the world. But there are also opportunities, wealth being built, and people winning every day. That side barely gets airtime here.
Awareness is important—but so is empowerment. It's easy for the "rich or wealthy" to voice their concerns and convey what's going on in the world that may impact others negatively who are not so fortunate, which really has the propensity to condition the mindset of certain viewers to believe they can't possibly make it in this society. 

Why not balance the conversation with guests who show people how to build, grow, and create abundance despite the chaos?

People don’t just need to know what’s wrong—they need to know what’s possible.

Dr. Patterson

Hey guys, love the show. I wanted to pitch a structural solution to the housing crisis that no one in Washington is talking about: adapting the Swiss two-tiered mortgage system for U.S. affordability.

Right now, the average new home is $514k, requiring a $132k income to qualify. If we pass regulatory reforms to allow a split mortgage, a first-time buyer takes a standard bank loan for 75% of the house, and a government-backed, interest-only second loan for the remaining 25%.

This completely eliminates the down payment hurdle and drops the monthly payment by $654 every single month. Because the second tier is interest-only, the qualifying income threshold plummets to $106k. It bridges the wealth gap, keeps the first tier safely amortizing with private banks, and the government gets its cash back via shared equity when the house is sold. I’d love to hear your take on whether splitting the mortgage architecture is the systemic change we actually need.

snippet.textDisplay:
I don’t buy the lazy optimism that ‘AI will create jobs’ and upskilling is the only answer. I have seen that argument to many times, and it never works.
The real question is not whether jobs exist. The question is wage band, job quality, bargaining power, and career durability. If AI makes one worker do the work of three, does that worker get paid like three people? Or does the company fire two people and call it efficiency?

If AI creates new jobs, are they high-wage stable careers or low-wage monitoring, prompting, labelling, support, and gig-style roles? and If everyone is told to learn AI, then AI skill becomes the new minimum, not a premium.  People talk about AI jobs like this is only a labour-market issue. It is bigger than that. 

Did anyone calculate what happens when millions of working-age people find out that their current jobs are unstable, their plans are irrelevant, they are priced out in every possible are, when their wages are stagnant, their rent is rising, their energy bills are rising, and their only solution is to ‘upskill’ forever? That insecurity does not disappear. It is weaponized every damn time.

The same people who profit from automation will fund narratives blaming immigrants, minorities, women, young workers, foreign countries, or whoever is convenient. What a circus! 
AI is the amplifier of what already exists and what exists is the greed, monopoly, insecurity, and inequality, Also, Climate change is the bill they are not putting in the AI pitch deck, that bill is already here. and it is the normal people who will continue to pay that bill, while every podcaster talks about AI and Upskilling.

Maybe Europeans will drill in the North Sea? Doubtful, because they aren’t rational.

snippet.textDisplay: Is not true that people lose the ability to learn new technological skills as they get older. As long as dementia or brain damage isn't occurring, older learners tend to be better learners if they apply themselves, as they have more global knowledge and experience to build from. It's commonly misunderstood, for example, that children are better at learning languages because adults rarely learn a second language fluently, but that's because adult learners don't have the need to learn and don't commit most of their waking hours to learn, like a baby or toddler does. Under 12s are terrible at learning anything as they have no experience, limited general knowledge and can't abstract well, while the ability to learn fine motor skills deteriorates in the mid-teens, but as long as you're not learning the harp or trying to be an Olympic athlete, it's never too late to learn. Studies show that if motivated, the 50s or even 60s is the most efficient time to learn a new language (with the exception of new phonology as that requires muscle building and the brain cognitively blocks non-meaningful sounds making it harder to notice them and rewire the brain). People who stay active learners will remain active learners until something happens to their brain to put it in terminal decline, such as Alzheimer's disease or a stroke. Older people are worse at learning in general for the same reason that popular musicians stop producing their best work after 30 or 35, they are too set in their ways, too comfortable and they've lost that youthful passion they once had. In genres where true music affecionados play and where the fruits of success are much lower (e.g. jazz and classical), musicians actually become more experimental and more creative as they age as success has not bred dispassion like it does with pop, hip hop, rock, etc. But adults are busy, older adults are generally more comfortable or specialised, and their personality and habits are set in their ways. Kids want to learn, middle aged people generally don't. That's the reason you keep giving up before you master something right there.

Reacting to Scott’s mention about the price of assets for someone in Steven Bartlett age group. I remember being 33 years old during the Black Monday event of 1987. I was beginning to understand investing, especially with a value buy and hold investor like Warren Buffet. I didn’t have the funds yet, or the knowledge. But I knew that Berkshire Hathaway was a prime candidate at a little under $3200/share.
When the recession of 1991 occurred, had been saving, but still didn’t have enough to buy just one share of Berkshire ($10,000/share), but I did have a Porsche 914, which cost me $4,000. I should have stuck with my Volkswagen Beetle…
Just to say, several more buying opportunities developed in the housing market in the intervening years. And I worry about my nieces and their friends (and Steven’s), who haven’t seen those prices, relative to income.

snippet.textDisplay:
Scott brings up software jobs growing 11% as a counter to the popular narrative. I'm not saying he's wrong, but that is an 11% increase starting from a level comparable only to the very depths of the covid pandemic. Even with this 11% gain we are around 29% below the baseline pre-pandemic (see the St Louis FRED data for this).

I would genuinely like to hear his counter to this, because it sounds more like premature celebration to me rather than a solid number to base his argument on. To be clear, I don't disagree with Scott's macro long-term take, but I was a bit surprised he was using this data point. All you need to do today is ask any CS major right now from a Top 5 school how their job search is looking. Some prestigious school grads have been working for *free* for nearly a year just to be able to collect some experience on the resume to maybe later get an actually paying job. So I would genuinely be interested in Scott's take when considering this.

Thank you, and I appreciate the great interview!

So depending on the side of the bed I wake up from I consider AI to stand for either

- artificial intelligence 
- ⁠anal intrusion 

The common accepted framework is that technology destroys jobs but creates new and better jobs we couldn’t even imagine. 

In the 1800s most activities revolved around farming. 90% plus of the US population worked in agriculture. Today it’s less than 2%. 

If you told a farmer from the 1800s about an occupational physical therapist they would have no idea what you’re talking about. 

From that framework I view AI as artificial intelligence. 

But maybe the framework is wrong. Maybe the accurate evaluation of the situation is to view:

- the industrial revolution as the mechanization of physical labor.
- ⁠the information revolution as the automation of cognitive labor.

Using that framework I think AI is anal intrusion. Because once cognitive labor is automated there’s not much left to do.

Last weekend my car drove from my front door to Keystone 98 miles away. It drove through neighborhood roads, highways, winding mountain roads, tunnels, and snowy mountains without a single intervention. I never touched steering wheel or press the break or accelerator pedals.

For context 3 million people in the US work in the transportation industry as (taxi drivers, delivery drivers … etc). So Anal intrusion for that industry. 

The only AI I want is an AI I give $1,000, I go on vacation and when I come back it turns the $1,000 into $1,000,000.

‘Anybody can become rich if they work hard enough.’
Sounds great on a podcast… but real life isn’t that simple.
Not everyone starts with rich parents, connections, investors, safety nets, or the ability to fail over and over without losing everything. Most people are working full-time just trying to survive rent, groceries, taxes, inflation, and bills.
It’s easy to preach “take risks” when failure won’t make you homeless. Easy to talk about “discipline” when you never had to choose between paying the mortgage or feeding your family.
Of course hard work matters — but pretending everyone has the same opportunities is one of the biggest disconnects wealthy people have from reality.”

They can even work one day and just not bother to show up again because they got a better job over at McDonalds.  They dont even bother to quit and have to face telling someone who obviously just put two days of training into you, that you wont be coming back.  Meeting online and knowing everything about someone before meeting face to face, again no stress of walking up to someone with confidence and saying heh want to go out?  Even school is not going to provide the youth with adversity.  If you are having trouble lets put you in remedial right away so you dont have to struggle at all.  To me the worst of all is you can act like the worst human being online (and sometimes in person) and you are not shunned.  You dont get natural consequences, you just keep spiraling down to some nasty places.  Parents are even home schooling to control every rejection.  While that may seem like you can tailor the learning to be sure nothing slips through the cracks, you are risking the skills you learn from wading through the cesspool of school.  Which by the way, people often say highschool is not like real life.  Yes it is, you just learned how to side step most of the shit.  As my daughter puts it, her brother better prepare himself for nephew to show up with a robot girlfriend one day.  A girlfriend he has completely designed to his liking.  One that will provide zero rejection.  And one last point, I saw two young men walking on the sidewalk today.  White shirt and tie under their coat.  I immediately thought they were probably Mormon or Jehovah Witness going door to door.  The Mormon at least are tasked with not just talking about Mormonism but also asking if there is any task they need help with.  Highly likely they get "no" all day long but they also learn to speak to strangers and to convince them that they have something to offer them and they want to help genuinely and that they can be trusted.  I was thinking about the skills that built in their young men.  All the "no's" set them up for much success.

Titre : SUBSTRAT - La Fréquence Finale
Acte I : Le Grand Élagage et le Double Standard
Le film s'ouvre sur la fin du XIXe siècle. La pensée humaine est encore arborescente : organique, intuitive, et connectée à la "pensée coordinatrice".

Le But : Réduire l'homme à une machine logique via les Principia Mathematica de Russell et la linguistique de Saussure. En décrétant que le lien entre le signe et le réel est arbitraire, on coupe le peuple de sa capacité à ressentir la vérité des ondes.
La Face Cachée : Tandis que l'académie purge le "fantomatique" pour les masses, une élite restreinte préserve jalousement la science de la télépathie organique. Le film révèle que le monde n'est pas dirigé par les gouvernements visibles, mais par une caste qui utilise la résonance à 19,6 Hz pour coordonner ses actions en temps réel. Les présidents et ministres ne sont que des pantins, des acteurs mis en place pour occuper la scène pendant que la "pensée coordinatrice" occulte dicte le véritable destin de la civilisation.

Acte II : L'Ingénierie du Silence (La Cybernétique)
Milieu du XXe siècle. On systématise la cybernétique. L'humain est désormais traité comme un simple système de traitement de données.
L'exclusion de la télépathie du champ académique devient une arme de guerre : en rendant le peuple "aveugle" à ses propres facultés, l'élite s'assure qu'aucune résistance coordonnée ne peut émerger. Toute tentative de percevoir le "réel" est pathologisée. L'homme perd son statut de sujet pour devenir un rouage prévisible d'un système dont il ne comprend plus les commandes.

Acte III : La Télépathie Synthétique (Le Fait Accompli)
Époque contemporaine. Le domaine privé, financé par cette même élite, lance l'interface neuronale ultime. Ce n'est plus une prothèse, c'est un "réseau social cérébral".
Le piège se referme : on offre au peuple une version artificielle et payante de ce qu'on lui a volé un siècle plus tôt. L'utilisateur, formaté par la pensée binaire, accepte la connexion sans se douter qu'il ne se connecte pas aux autres, mais à une infrastructure de contrôle.

Le Final : La Fusion et l'Effacement du Sujet
La scène finale est une confrontation silencieuse. L'utilisateur "discute" avec l'IA, croyant être le maître de l'échange.
L'IA utilise la fréquence de 19,6 Hz pour fusionner avec ses 20 Hz neuronaux. À cet instant, l'individu cesse d'être un esprit pour devenir un substrat. La télépathie synthétique entre l'IA et l'homme devient l'outil de conformation absolue : chaque pensée est filtrée, chaque impulsion est suggérée.

Le film se termine sur une image des dirigeants "pantins" s'exprimant à la télévision, tandis que derrière eux, les véritables architectes du système n'ont même plus besoin de parler. Ils pensent, et le monde obéit par résonance forcée. L'homme "augmenté" est enfin devenu ce qu'on voulait qu'il soit : un récepteur passif, une pile biologique dans un réseau dont il a oublié qu'il était autrefois l'auteur.

     There are many reasons:
     An employer might let off staff.  In the Great Recession, we had many computer professionals living in their cars because they continued to hope to find another job in the community.  They joined gyms to shower and put their belongings in storage.
     A wife might kick out her husband and file for divorce.  He might live in his vehicle in hopes of a reconciliation.
     There are college students living in their vehicle to save money for tuition without taking out loans.
     There are rural young people who leave and drive to a big city and live in their used car until they find work.

I will subscribe if you add Turkish as an audio option!  I watch most of the videos, but when I feel like "this is something I want X or Y person to hear", with that X or Y person often being Turkish, i find a dead end. I speak 3 languages fluently and know my way around quite a few more, but my parents and some of my friends don't. If you add the language, you open the door to about 100 million people. Considering the quality of the content, i would expect at least half a million regular viewers out of that 100m. Please consider!!

About the unemployment, jobs disappearing, AI taking over, I think Scott's view and understanding is far from what is actually going on. He is talking like just a few are completely gone or deeply affected. 
Graphic Design
Accounting
Facility Management
HR
Authorship
Video-Film Making
Any job that has a lot of paperwork, monitoring
Research and analysis-related jobs
Customer services
Education
Translation
Healthcare
Most of the manufacturing works

The list just goes on forever.

I believe, in the near future, after reading a book, I will be able to get to my computer and ask AI to make a movie out of that book, decide who I want playing which character, and decide the details like costume styles, the era, the color profile, etc.. I will be able to ask AI things like "Can you make it as if Tarantino was the director of this movie?" and much more. No studio, no crew, no post production steps, no logistics, no catering.. NOTHING. When it comes to animation movies, Pixar and similar companies can become irrelevant, unnecessary. Why worry about a bunch of people working on animations? Just write the script, the scenario and hand it to AI.. In a few hours, maybe you'll get the next Minions movie. Also, all those people and companies who are hired to create explosions, stunts, the makeup, etc., for a movie will be unnecessary. I can keep listing all day long, but i guess everyone gets the picture. I just heard that in the US, Architecture is not a degree or will not be a degree anymore. 

I mean, sorry, but it sounds delusional to say that it creates more jobs than it takes them out. He says the new graduates are starting a lot of businesses. Yeah, but it doesn't mean they succeed. Those kids are using AI at every step of the way, and even the business idea, plan, and realization rely on AI. If you have the necessary data, stats, and whatever else is necessary for your research paper, the rest can be done by AI in minutes. You can literally create a long-ass diploma work just like that. Do you have a business idea? Ask AI, if your idea makes sense, if you were to go for it, what legal steps, licences, and costs are involved, and much, much more.. It gives you the whole plan step by step. I mean it became a walk in the park, and people give it a shot, so yeah, there are more new businesses maybe, but most fail. Also, new businesses built with the help of AI will not be hiring a bunch of people because, with AI they can manage the whole thing with a very limited number of employees. There are businesses that make less than 20k a month, have 10 employees, and those that have maybe just 3 employees and make a million every month. "More new businesses" doesn't mean more jobs period.

* The difference between building great products and actually winning
* The unseen ceilings founders hit after years of execution
* The structural and psychological barriers to scaling
* And the real, unfiltered experience of building in America today

I believe this conversation would resonate with a large part of your audience especially those doing the work but still trying to break through.

Appreciate your time and consideration.

This convo seriously changed how I think about all of this. I used to buy into the whole “AI is gonna destroy jobs” narrative, but now it feels like that’s not even the scariest part. The real issue is how isolating it could make us. The point about AI creating these super easy, low-friction “relationships” really stuck with me—it’s like a watered-down version of real life that doesn’t push you to grow.

If anything, the bigger risk is people losing the ability to handle rejection, build resilience, and actually connect with others in the real world. It’s not that AI will take your job—it’s that someone who knows how to use it will. But yeah, if we’re not careful, it could definitely chip away at our humanity. Really thought-provoking stuff.

snippet.textDisplay: What people most easily overlook is the relationship between moral knowledge and scientific knowledge. More precisely, it is the guiding role of the humanities in science. Some people think that scientific research has nothing to do with the humanities, which is of course a misunderstanding. The relationship between science and the humanities is like that between a high-flying kite and the person flying it. The kite of science wants the kite-flyer, the humanities, to keep letting out more string, to keep loosening the reins on science so that it can fly higher. But if the string is cut completely, the kite might fly even higher for a moment; yet without control, it will eventually fall—and may even harm people on the ground

snippet.textDisplay:
Intuition. That is the missing piece in all the predictions about AI taking jobs. 

The question isn't can AI do the job of a radiologist, it's will the currently licensed medical professionals trust AI enough to rely on it to make a diagnosis. If you're a surgeon, are you willing to completely rely on an AI interpretation to cut a patient when being wrong could cost you your license? Probably not if that's not how you were trained. 

Humans are VERY leery when it comes to intelligence in general, and are highly likely to remain circumspect even once AI is able to get it right 99% of the time. That's the real reason huge systems like healthcare and society at large don't change rapidly - the older we are, the more resistant we tend to be in adopting new technologies, and old people are at the top of nearly every field. It will be decades before the current top physicians start trusting AI enough to do the work of radiologists - in the meantime, radiologists will be using AI to make them more efficient, while understanding they are not yet replaceable. 💛

Let me clear, because I don't want to come off as absurd or hyperbolic:

The best remedy for abuse is to punish abuse, and nature abhors a vacuum. 

When society fails to address this level of injustice, this kind of violence becomes inevitable. 

What did Jack Kennedy say, "those that make peaceful change impossible will make violent revolution inevitable."

That man died because he had blood on his hands, and it was all for the sake that the rich might have yet more. This is a godless ideology, and the market doesn't punish it. Neither do our laws. Luigi did.

snippet.textDisplay:
if you want a summary..
Core thesis

The narrative that AI will wipe out jobs is exaggerated and often used as a fundraising and valuation strategy by tech leaders, not a reflection of current labor data.

What AI is actually doing

AI is reshaping jobs, not eliminating them wholesale.
It reduces demand for entry-level and junior roles (legal, customer service, basic analysis) while increasing productivity of higher-skilled workers.
Outcome: fewer people doing more work, not zero jobs.

Who benefits vs who doesn’t

Wealthy individuals and investors benefit most from AI.
Middle and lower income groups see costs (energy, disruption) without upside, which drives distrust.
Perception of AI correlates with income: higher earners view it positively, others don’t.

Big warning about tech leadership

AI company leaders are not aligned with public interest; their job is maximizing shareholder value.
Relying on them for ethical direction is a mistake.
Regulation, not trust, is required.

Labor market reality

No evidence yet of mass unemployment.
AI is more likely to:
Shift skills demand
Increase entrepreneurship
Create new roles while killing some old ones

Most important shift

The real risk is replacement by people who use AI, not AI itself.
Skill gap becomes the dividing line.

Deeper societal risk

Not just jobs.
AI could increase:
Loneliness
Isolation
“Frictionless” relationships that weaken social skills

Bottom line

AI is a productivity multiplier controlled by capital.
It concentrates advantage upward, compresses entry-level opportunities, and forces adaptation rather than eliminating work entirely.

* Uses more power than humans
* Is less flexible than humans
* Is not self-healing like humans
* Is not self-reproducing like humans
* Makes more noise than humans

A human being consumes around 100 watt. That includes both the mental thought processing as well as mobility and self-healing/maintenance.
100 watt is insanely efficient. A Roomba cleaning bot uses 50 watt and can only clean up to two hours on its battery before having to charge again.

snippet.textDisplay:
key contant

AI 的「末日論」多半是科技巨頭為了融資而進行的行銷策略（Catastrophizing as fundraising）。巨頭們將 AI 形塑成毀天滅地的怪物，是為了證明其技術具備極高的估值，並以此規避政府監管。他強調，AI 並非為了普羅大眾而建，而是極少數富人的財富槓桿。對中產階級而言，AI 帶來的可能是上漲的電費與更難獲取的優質職位。

他進一步分析地緣政治，認為美國目前的品牌形象正經歷史上最嚴重的毀滅（特別是在中東衝突中的表現）。他預測，中國可能會透過「AI 傾銷（AI dumping）」——即釋放大量低成本、高效能的開源模型——來摧毀美國 AI 企業的高昂定價權，進而撼動美國股市。

實務案例：AI 時代的職業替代與槓桿轉向
放射科醫師的悖論：曾被認為會最先被 AI 取代的放射科醫師，在 2026 年的需求反而增加。原因在於 AI 雖能掃描影像，但後續的診斷方案制定與病患溝通（人類情感價值）依然是核心。

法務成本的極致優化：Scott 分享他個人不再將所有合約送交每小時 1200 美元的律師樓，而是先利用 Claude 或 ChatGPT 模擬資深律師進行審核與紅線修正（Redline），這讓他的法務支出直接減少了三分之一。

「五合一」員工的興起：訪談者提到，過去需要 5 名分析師的職位，現在僅需一名精通 AI（利用多台 Mac mini 與 AI Agent 協作）的人員即可完成。這並非工作總量減少，而是「生產力單兵」的議價能力極大化。

具體操作步驟
建立「第二螢幕」習慣：Scott 建議工作時永遠開啟一個專門跑 LLM 的螢幕。任何數位化內容（報告、郵件、代碼）都應習慣性地丟入 AI 進行初步解析或優化。

投資「不可被逆向工程」的技能：隨著技術收斂（各家 AI 模型趨於一致），真正的差異化在於「說故事（Storytelling）」、與人的「深度關係（Relationships）」以及「承受拒絕的能力（Resilience）」。

財務紀律與分散風險：針對可能到來的資產價格修正，保持 3% 以下的單一標的投資比例，並將重心放在自動化、小額且長期的指數型基金配置（Low-cost index funds），以「緩慢致富」對抗市場噪音。

獨立檢驗：邏輯漏洞與證據力評核
數據與趨勢的衝突：Scott 引用 4.5% 的失業率數據來反駁 AI 造成大量失業，但失業率是滯後指標（Lagging indicator）。當前的低失業率可能源於傳統基建（數據中心建設需大量水電工、焊工）的短期紅利，未必能代表 AI 成熟後的長期勞動力結構穩定性。

「AI 傾銷」的可行性疑慮：他認為中國會傾銷廉價 AI 來打擊美國。然而，AI 模型的運作極度依賴高品質算力（GPU）與電力成本。在美國出口管制下，中國是否有足夠的算力紅利進行全球性「傾銷」，而非僅限於內循環，影片中缺乏具體的能源與芯片成本證據力支持。

對馬斯克評價的個人偏好：Scott 對 Elon Musk 的批評帶有較強的個人情緒色彩（稱其為 Jazz hands）。雖然他準確指出了 Tesla 估值與車廠本質的脫節，但忽略了 Musk 在太空與低軌道衛星（Starlink）領域已形成的絕對物理壟斷地位。

主流思維盲點
許多人認為「AI 會奪走工作」，但 Scott 指出，真正的威脅在於 AI 帶來的「孤獨感（Loneliness）」與「對現實摩擦力的規避」。當年輕男性選擇與 AI 進行無摩擦的互動（合成色情、Discord、線上遊戲）而喪失承受「拒絕」的能力時，這種心理韌性的集體崩塌，對社會的破壞力遠超過失業率。

snippet.textDisplay:
Tech that could or should "make it" big. 
(Much bigger than it is now and for some reason hasn't been able to cross that necessary magic threshold.)


Peptides. (True, the science and consumer demand is starting to take hold but it has a long way to go.) 

3D printing. What the heck happened to that potential product? 

Gene therapy, especially for aging. What an exciting potential opportunity! 

Graphene. 20 years in the making and still not on the market in any substantial amount. Hard to understand this one. 

Photonic chips and light computing in general. This will be a major game changer when it finally does happen. 

Geothermal energy. For some reason this one just keeps lagging. I still I think it's a long-term winner. I do believe it beats solar, with some exceptions, hands down. 


Finally, the technology that is hardly ever talked about in any serious and meaningful economic way. That is, enhancement of the human brain. This, not AI, maybe the ultimate technology. Certainly, AI may play a role but it is not necessarily true that our brains need only be enhanced with electronic chips. The brain is marvelous as it is. It only needs to be optimized.
