snippet.textDisplay:
This is the AI conversation people need because it avoids both traps.
Trap one: “AI will destroy every job and humans are obsolete.”
Trap two: “AI is just another tool and everyone should stop worrying.”
The truth is more structural.
AI is a productivity engine being deployed through concentrated capital. That means the most important question is not whether AI is good or bad in the abstract.
The real questions are:
Who owns the models?
Who owns the chips?
Who owns the data centers?
Who pays the energy cost?
Who captures the productivity gain?
Who gets laid off first?
Who gets retrained?
Who regulates the companies?
Who audits the systems?
Who is liable when AI causes harm?
Galloway’s strongest point is that we should not be asking whether we can “trust” Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Dario Amodei, Zuckerberg, or any other tech CEO. We should not need to trust them.
Their job is not public welfare. Their job is shareholder value, market dominance, valuation, and capital access.
That is why regulation matters.
The AI CEOs sell two stories at once:
    1. This technology is so powerful it may transform or destabilize society.
    2. But also, trust us to deploy it at private-company speed with public consequences.
No.
If AI is powerful enough to reshape jobs, elections, media, education, surveillance, warfare, medicine, and social life, then it is powerful enough to require democratic oversight.
The job question also needs precision.
AI may not create instant mass unemployment tomorrow. But it can still hollow out entry-level work, compress five jobs into one AI-enabled worker, destroy training ladders, and shift bargaining power toward owners.
That is not apocalypse. It is class restructuring.
The public does not need doom. The public needs ownership, retraining, labor protections, audit rights, energy accountability, privacy law, antitrust enforcement, and elected officials who understand the technology well enough to regulate it.
AI was not built as a democratic public utility.

This is the AI conversation people need because it avoids both traps.
Trap one: “AI will destroy every job and humans are obsolete.”
Trap two: “AI is just another tool and everyone should stop worrying.”
The truth is more structural.
AI is a productivity engine being deployed through concentrated capital. That means the most important question is not whether AI is good or bad in the abstract.
The real questions are:
Who owns the models?
Who owns the chips?
Who owns the data centers?
Who pays the energy cost?
Who captures the productivity gain?
Who gets laid off first?
Who gets retrained?
Who regulates the companies?
Who audits the systems?
Who is liable when AI causes harm?
Galloway’s strongest point is that we should not be asking whether we can “trust” Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Dario Amodei, Zuckerberg, or any other tech CEO. We should not need to trust them.
Their job is not public welfare. Their job is shareholder value, market dominance, valuation, and capital access.
That is why regulation matters.
The AI CEOs sell two stories at once:
    1. This technology is so powerful it may transform or destabilize society.
    2. But also, trust us to deploy it at private-company speed with public consequences.
No.
If AI is powerful enough to reshape jobs, elections, media, education, surveillance, warfare, medicine, and social life, then it is powerful enough to require democratic oversight.
The job question also needs precision.
AI may not create instant mass unemployment tomorrow. But it can still hollow out entry-level work, compress five jobs into one AI-enabled worker, destroy training ladders, and shift bargaining power toward owners.
That is not apocalypse. It is class restructuring.
The public does not need doom. The public needs ownership, retraining, labor protections, audit rights, energy accountability, privacy law, antitrust enforcement, and elected officials who understand the technology well enough to regulate it.
AI was not built as a democratic public utility.
That is the problem.

snippet.textDisplay: AI’s strength is pattern recognition like training on radiological scans against known results. However, at some point you have to stop training because it will begin making assumptions beyond its capability (currently referred to as Hallucinations but better described as thinking it thinks it is smarter than it is and begins making assumptions). We all know people like that (maybe I am one) 😮 Once this occurs, how do you undo it? You can start over, attempt to train out of it or use code as a gatekeeper between the AI model and its solutions. All are messy or very time consuming because you have no way of knowing how the model learned what it knows. I suspect all three methods are used. I also suspect the training of large language models involves periodically stopping training along the way to save what you have at that time, so you can go back to where the model last seemed to work best before overtraining was discovered . Another challenge is say you built a model to list the chemicals say in something like storm runoff from a city or factory. Once a new chemical is introduced, the AI model at best is severely compromised but most likely useless. Having said all of this, I believe large language models have far greater issues than those trained on pattern type data and they will never be something that should be cut loose without constraints. snippet.textDisplay:
Before blindly following Scott Galloway’s worldview, people should recognize the incentive structure underneath it.

He is not merely analyzing American decline. His public positioning, investments, and media persona often benefit from amplifying instability, pessimism, institutional distrust, and generational resentment. There is a difference between warning your country about risk and building an identity around profiting from national deterioration narratives.

That distinction matters.

Criticism of the United States is healthy. Betting against its resilience while continuing to extract wealth, influence, and status from the very system you frame as collapsing is something else entirely. At some point, the line between analyst and accelerant begins to blur.

You do not strengthen a civilization by endlessly convincing its people that everything is broken beyond repair. Constant collapse rhetoric becomes culturally corrosive, especially when delivered from positions of extreme wealth and insulation.

And ironically, the market has buried this worldview repeatedly across history. America has flaws—serious ones—but betting on its total failure has historically been one of the most expensive long-term positions a person can take.

As for the personal branding side of things, let’s also stop pretending influence, wealth, power, and status are the same thing as raw physical attraction. Mature adults understand social dynamics are multi-variable. Success changes perceived attractiveness. That’s not shocking; that’s civilization since the invention of agriculture.

But conflating status-based attraction with pure physical desirability is ego inflation, not honesty.

Critique systems. Critique incentives. Critique narratives.

But don’t confuse cynicism for wisdom just because it’s packaged with confidence and a podcast microphone.

I've been a fan of the show and Scott specifically for a while now. I have a lot of love for Scott as a thought leader for his radically pragmatic outlook on what all is going on... Thank you Scott for the amazing interview and the powerful words and thank you Steven as always for running the best podcast on the platform!

snippet.textDisplay:
The most profitable AI product right now is not software.
It is certainty packaged as a story.

Scott is right to push back on the “AI job apocalypse” script. The real issue is not whether AI is powerful. It is who captures the upside, who absorbs the downside, and how fear gets used to raise capital, accelerate adoption, and delay accountability.

A few things matter here:
Fear converts faster than nuance, so the message gets simplified.

Entry level roles get squeezed first because those jobs often contain the tasks AI can compress.

Productivity gains do not automatically become higher wages. They usually become higher margins unless workers have leverage.

“Trust the founder” is not a governance model.

The winners will be people who combine domain skill, judgment, communication, and relationship capital.


The near-term risk is not that every job disappears overnight.

The real risk is role compression, wage pressure, fewer career ladders, and more people feeling replaceable while the upside compounds upward.

Do this next: audit one workflow you own. Use AI to reduce the mechanical work, but keep ownership of the judgment, ethics, relationships, and final decision.

That is the real leverage.

Where do you think the first major value shift lands: labor, capital, or regulation?

snippet.textDisplay:
We are collectively underwriting the rise of artificial intelligence. Every interaction, dataset, and fragment of human expression becomes training material—an ongoing, unpaid contribution to systems that derive their value from aggregated human knowledge, both historical and contemporary.
At the same time, the economic rewards generated from these systems are being concentrated in the hands of a small group of executives and shareholders, many of whom are amassing extraordinary wealth. That asymmetry raises a legitimate question: if AI systems are built on the intellectual and behavioral capital of humanity at large, should there not be some form of distributed compensation or structural return to the public?
What’s particularly striking is the rhetoric from certain voices who criticize AI leadership for ethical detachment or for “crossing to the dark side.” Yet, when you examine their own framing—how they speak about scale, control, and profit—they often reflect the same underlying posture they claim to oppose. The critique becomes less a moral stance and more a repositioning within the same system

snippet.textDisplay:
We should really be having an honest conversation about whether electric vehicles are actually good for the planet.

Personally, I’m not convinced they are. There are real concerns around cobalt mining, low-paid and sometimes exploitative labor, including child labor, and the environmental impact of toxic chemicals. In some ways, it feels like we’re just shifting pollution to different places rather than solving the problem. Issues like nuclear waste and groundwater contamination also deserve attention.

At the same time, I understand that fossil fuels have caused serious environmental damage, along with conflict and human suffering. I just think we need to evaluate electric transportation with the same level of scrutiny we apply to fossil fuels and make thoughtful, side-by-side comparisons.

A lot of the current conversation feels driven by hype, and I’m not sure everyone has fully considered the bigger picture. That said, this is just my perspective, and I’m open to being wrong.

snippet.textDisplay: Here's a counterpoint though (just playing devil's advocate since I don't actually believe that AI is going to replace nearly as many humans as a lot of people believe it will, nor lead to economic collapse): if indeed it is the case that the number of humans needed to maintain (or even increase) our productivity is going to decline over time, then is this not perfectly timed with the fact that human reproduction is ALSO declining?  Scott mentioned the incredible advances in Chinese industrial automation.  Why was China SO ahead of the curve on this?  They noticed years ago that their birthrates are far sub-replacement just like ours, and for a largely middle-income economy that relies on industrial production, a shortage of labor would be fatal.  Japanese companies are obsessed with robotics and automation for exactly the same reason—the Japanese population has been declining for decades now, and yet they manage to maintain roughly the same output of goods and services.  Is it not too perfect that as time goes on, as the number of workers available to work declines, so too will automation reduce our need for human labor?  Fewer jobs + more people = bad.  Fewer jobs + fewer people = good/neutral.

snippet.textDisplay: @MajICReiki Ugh, I wish this narrative would go away already.  Fertility decline has NOTHING TO DO with economics!! NHTSA has two open investigations covering 3.2 million Tesla vehicles. One was escalated to a formal Engineering Analysis in March after 9 crashes, including a fatality, where the system FAILED to detect sun glare, fog, and dust. The cameras went blind and the car kept driving.

In Austin, Tesla's robotaxi fleet has reported 15 crashes across roughly 800,000 miles. One crash every 57,000 miles. 

The average American driver has a police-reported crash every 500,000 miles. Tesla's robotaxis crash at roughly 4x the human rate, WITH a safety monitor sitting in the car whose only job is to prevent crashes.

snippet.textDisplay:
Tesla isn’t really a car company. It’s a software, AI, and data company that happens to sell cars as a distribution platform. The vehicles are just sensors on wheels feeding a massive data pipeline.

They overpromise timelines—consistently—but they do eventually ship. That matters more than perfect execution. No one else is operating at their scale of real-world data collection.

Layer on SpaceX, X (formerly Twitter), and xAI, and you get something more important than a “monopoly”—you get vertical integration across compute, distribution, communications, and physical infrastructure. That’s leverage most competitors simply don’t have.

Even if only a fraction of their roadmap materializes, they’re still years ahead in key domains like autonomy and applied AI. Most competitors are reacting, not leading.

Now the uncomfortable part: labor.

White-collar automation is accelerating faster than labor markets can realistically absorb. That’s not hypothetical—it’s already happening. The idea that displaced workers smoothly transition into new roles at scale is optimistic at best. Historically, these transitions lag by years or decades.

But the “everything collapses into total control” angle is overcooked. Governments and large corporations will gain influence—no question—but absolute control isn’t how these systems behave. Power fragments as often as it concentrates, especially when multiple nation-states and corporations compete.

Physical labor doesn’t save the equation either. If white-collar displacement pushes into blue-collar sectors, supply spikes and wages compress. That’s basic market mechanics. There will be work—but not necessarily enough high-quality work.

On education: there’s some truth, but your take is too broad. The system does over-index on standardized testing and short-term performance metrics. That produces shallow competence instead of deep understanding. But writing off an entire generation as “weak and dumb” is just noise. There are plenty of highly capable people coming up—they’re just unevenly distributed.

The real issue isn’t intelligence—it’s attention. Short-form content loops degrade focus, which directly impacts critical thinking and skill depth over time. That’s a structural problem, not a generational flaw.

Bottom line:
The future isn’t a clean utopia or a total collapse. It’s asymmetric—massive gains for those positioned correctly, real pain for those who aren’t. That’s where things are actually headed.

And yes—being both excited and uneasy about that trajectory is the rational position.

I feel like he's romanticizing the ability for everyone to use AI to setup a business. A lot of the time when a new business enters a market, it's not because the current market leaders were unaware of a gap, it's because they didn't have the knowledge or expertise to exploit it. 

For example if i run a top Aircraft leasing company focused on planes, I might be aware there's an opportunity to enter the helicopter industry, but i know nothing about helicopters, none of my staff know anything about helicopters, so to explore the opportunity i'd have to divert staff and resources away from the existing business or hire new staff etc. This would be a bad idea because it would be pure speculation and diverting attention away from my real business. Historically this left gaps in markets where maybe a guy that worked in the helicopter industry, that had a big network in the industry, could come in and set up a business and take that market share. But now i have an AI program that knows everything there is to know about helicopters, accounting for helicopters, legal nuances to the industry, it knows everything about my business, sales pipeline etc. and can come up with a business plan for me overnight on how to take advantage of the industry. So if i present my plan to investors, and so does the other guy. Who are they going to give the money to? Me who is an established name in the industry with a proven track record of running a successful business etc. or this other guy who has no collateral, no track record etc.? So basically, i feel like everyone having an AI will be irrelevant, because existing companies will have AI as well and just gobble up those gaps immediately.

Especially considering the scale of unemployment is going to dramatically reduce peoples disposable income. So right now, someone quitting their finance role to become a home baker, selling their cakes at a farmers market is lovely humble success story, but the reason they were a success is because everyone else is still in their high paying tech jobs willing to pay 20 euro for a carrot cake. When everyone is unemployed, people will barely be able to afford the 1 euro carrot cake in lidl.

snippet.textDisplay:
This is my go-to podcast every single week, so I say this with the utmost respect for what Steven and the team have built.
But when I see headlines like “AI wasn’t built for you” and “the rich don’t need you anymore,” my heart sinks a little. Because I’ve heard this story before. The Godfathers of AI,   Mo Gawdat and other brilliant guests, are all pointing in the same direction: most people are being left behind, wealth is concentrating at the top, and the rest of us should be worried. Message received. 
What I’d genuinely love to see is an episode that flips the script. Bring on a deeply hands-on AI engineer or a business owner who’s excelling in using AI. Perhaps you could even interview yourself, Steven, alongside your agent (s) or hologram. That would be brilliant. Not someone there to warn, but someone there to show. What tools should a CEO be using right now? How exactly does AI actually get implemented in a real business today? What do those workflows, playbooks, and exceptional prompts look like in practice?
This is The Diary of a CEO after all. Every CEO and aspiring CEO watching should be using these tools,  yet most people still don’t know where to start. There’s no shortage of fear. What’s missing is practical direction.
And here’s what gets lost in all of it: we’re living through one of the most significant shifts in how humans think, create, and operate. For the first time, capability is no longer tied to time, team size, or even technical skill in the same way. That changes everything.
We’ve seen this pattern before. When the internet emerged, early narratives focused on risk, job loss, disconnection, and power concentration. Some of that played out. But what mattered more was who learned to use it early. The internet didn’t just disrupt industries; it redistributed access. It gave individuals leverage that previously only institutions had.
AI feels like that moment again,  but much faster, and more personal. The gap won’t just be between rich and poor, but between those who engage with the tools and those who don’t.

snippet.textDisplay:
Ok so I’m not the only one who thinks this guy’s yet another blowhard talking as if he’s walked the walk.
IMO and from my experience - prompt engineering is only as good as your level of domain expertise.  And even that usually isn’t “good enough”.  Just ask the owner of that PocketOS startup that had ClaudeAI delete his production database in 9 seconds.  His full and incremental backups resided in the same volume that was deleted as well.  The same API key controlled all environments and either wasn’t encrypted or was provisioned without enough guardrails.
Now before doing anything I find myself debating over use cases, tech stack design constraints, security, cost, future proofing, etc before hitting the button to ‘GO code it now’.
But this is because I’ve built systems from the ground up for 30+ years.  Actually the guy at the keyboard… rummaging through documentation, tech forums, stack overflow, dev environments - open source and proprietary.
I feel for the folks entering this space or haven’t done the heavy lifting to know how this tech impacts or where to begin because blowhards like this guy are so convincing in their well articulated delivery.  They’re no different than the pie in the sky execs who sat down for a day with Gartner or Bearing Point and rubber stamped the ‘new way forward’, when all of my fellow engineers would scoff and knew it was doomed from the start.  Don’t talk as if you know everything if you haven’t done it.

snippet.textDisplay:
My take about AI; I’ve been working in IT for 26  years, and one thing never changes: people are always worried about their current job and uncertain about the future.

Every wave of new technology triggers the same reaction. Fear first. Then adaptation.

What actually happens is usually this:
- Some jobs disappear.
- Some jobs become more complex through layers of added complexity.
- Entirely new jobs emerge that didn’t exist before.

And interestingly enough, when you look back a few years later, many professionals end up becoming more valuable in the market because they adapted and evolved with the technology.


Technology changes the playing field. It rarely ends the game.

@Gosankyo

That’s a fair point, and I understand why people feel that way.

But history also shows that every generation believed the new technology would replace human value entirely. The Industrial Revolution replaced physical labor. Computers replaced administrative labor. Automation replaced repetitive labor.

AI is different because it also impacts cognitive work. That part is true.

But intelligence alone is not the same as judgment, responsibility, creativity, leadership, trust, context, or human relationships. Businesses still run on those things.

That’s exactly what I meant in my earlier comment about jobs becoming more complex through additional layers of complexity. That shift creates a major opportunity for people willing to keep learning and develop themselves

snippet.textDisplay: Most people (Scott included) who are not in the industry and yet who think AI will replace everyone and everything don't understand the tech, or its limitations.  There will never be AGI because LLMs are not actually 'intelligent' per se.  All they are doing is statistically predicting the next most likely token (word) in a string based on every string of words in every language that exists on the internet, kind of like how the TikTok algorithm tries to predict the next video it thinks you will probably want to watch based on every TikTok you have ever watched.  LLMs have no idea what the words actually mean, just in what order those words are statistically most likely to appear, which is why you can get very persuasive (and grammatically perfect) but otherwise factually dubious outputs (hallucinations).  Remember Gemini telling people how many rocks they should eat, or that people should glue their cheese to their pizza?  Well, scarcely any progress at all has been made on the hallucination problem.  Even on the most advanced frontier models they still get even obvious things wrong.  LLMs are groundbreaking technology, no doubt, but they are not (and never will be) "intelligent" in the same way humans are.  Never forget: LLMs are really (REALLY) good autocomplete machines, and nothing more.  Use them as such, and they can indeed improve your productivity, but don't base mission-critical decisions on the factual accuracy of anything an LLM tells you.  It doesn't 'know' what it's saying.

Unless you're deep in the 2025+ shift toward Agentic AI and autonomous coding, it’s just way too easy to underestimate the disruption because of two big mistakes:

First, there’s this 'Historical Analogy' Fallacy. We keep trying to group AI with past revolutions like the wheel, the printing press, or even the internet. But think about it: historically, humans always adapted to tools. They were passive instruments. What we’re seeing now is a radical departure from that. We aren't just building another tool to 'use'; we're witnessing the emergence of a self-directing entity—a form of intelligence that actually acts instead of just being operated.

Second is the 'Prediction Paradox'. People try to forecast a world with AGI or even ASI while completely ignoring the Singularity factor. It’s basically an event horizon. Once intelligence surpasses our biological capacity to even understand it, our current economic and social models just stop making sense. Trying to predict that future with today’s logic is like trying to see past the edge of a black hole—it’s just not possible.

That said, I do recognize the massive disconnect between market valuations and actual revenue right now. We’re likely in a bubble that’s bound to burst. But here’s the thing: a market correction doesn’t change the fundamental reality of the tech. It might change the 'when,' but it’ll never change the 'what.' The destination is the same; the timeline is just subject to the market being volatile.

Agree 100%. Also, the job problem may be the easiest to solve by simply shortening the work week. 

That's something we already did to create more jobs during the Great Depression in the 1930s, when we created an official workweek of 40 hours instead of the 80 hours most jobs then entailed.

To encourage employers to hire more workers rather than make their existing workers work longer hours, employers had to pay an hourly rate higher than the rate paid for the first 40 hours. 

To discourage workers from volunteering for overtime pay, the extra pay at a higher rate put them into a higher tax bracket, so they would take home less of the higher-rate pay than they got from being paid at the 40-hour rate.

If we now cut the workweek in response to A.I., worker pay and benefits can remain about the same as they were when one worker did the job without A.I., because this plan converts the increased productivity from A.I. into more personal time for workers, rather than into higher profits for the non-working rentier class.

We could cut the work week again. White-collar "management" jobs, which were not subject to the aforementioned overtime rules, used to come with certain privileges that have since been eroded; among these privileges was job security. It was an unwritten rule if you worked for IBM, for example, you had a job for life.

snippet.textDisplay:
Wow, I happen to be a radiologist. I’ve thought a lot about this, and this is a common misconception, radiologists are not at risk. We have a technical field, so Scott’s is a common misconception.  We are not impacted by AI in the way that you think. you still need someone to sue.. someone to take credit for the report. We have an academy that protects us — we invented this science and get to decide what makes a “radiologist.” Our academy sets the medical standard/requirements. 

I’m actually struggling with my employer because I want to work remotely more, and the hospital insists that I’m physically there. Surgeons still come in and need to speak directly with you. An MD with a physics background needs to step on a pedal and unleash a radiation dose. Someone needs to write prescriptions and sign papers. And I’ll add, the human mind remains a pretty impressive thing. A seasoned radiologist is often in owe of his own eyes, and can detect things that AI simply cannot detect now. We have more context. It truly will take general AI before that happens, and in that case, we’re all screwed. 

Currently, I use AI to detect pulmonary emboli and hemorrhage within the brain, and c spine fractures. These are three out of 10,000+ conditions that a radiologist can decipher using a real medical education once the eye detects the abnormality (not an algorithm trained on Wikipedia). I then use AI to draft my report into an impression. 

Radiology is similar to air traffic control. Our volumes have increased, the pressure has increased, entire industries have purchased us and make profit off our existence, and we make increasingly less money. The public has absolutely no idea how much pressure we are under. Big industry takes over but when mistakes happen, individual people fall on the sword. AI probably could help us, though, if it wasn’t going to inevitably all end up in the hands of 10 or less oligarchs on the spectrum. 

Don’t become a doctor. If you do, look into Radiology.

snippet.textDisplay:
The idea that “new jobs will appear, don’t worry” !! Sounds overly simplistic given the scale and speed of AI development. Unlike past technological shifts, AI is not just replacing manual labor  it is rapidly automating cognitive and creative work as well.
Entire sectors are already under pressure creative industries (writing, design, media), entry- and mid-level IT roles, routine tasks in finance and law, education and translation, customer service, logistics, manufacturing, and transport. The issue is not just job loss, but a structural gap new roles require different skills, and society cannot retrain fast enough.
More importantly, there is a deeper economic contradiction even if companies cut costs through automation, who will buy their products if fewer people have stable incomes? 
If the population shrinks or becomes less able to consume, mass production loses its foundation.
In the end, the real challenge is not technological, but systemic how to sustain demand, distribute value, and maintain economic balance in a world where human labor is no longer central.😮

snippet.textDisplay:
From my humble research, what I noticed specifically is that the rates at which the number of leaders in literally every sector of life globally that is increasing against the rate at which the number of employees are entering the workforce is ridiculous. Way more employees are entering the work force compared to the number of leaders that are being either promoted, people opening businesses and just to clarify, by leaders I mean business owners, owners of educational or professional training institutions and corporations. Corporations are a special case: Usually they operate in the format of board of directors. Now although having a board of directors rather than a single owner is obviously a better thing, one fact that needs to be pointed out is that the difference in the number of board of directors in the corporations to the number of their employees has increased exponentially if you look at the last 20 years. 

The Stock Market IPO Boom was one of those places where most of these employees went after years of growing dissentment after witnessing the growing divide of wealth between each of them and their leader counterparts. We all know what happens to most the of minority stakeholders: they make a very little margin of profit, if any at all compared to the big stakeholders, often the board of directors of these corporations. 

I found 2 possible solutions, many which are already being used in many countries today: 

1. Governments worldwide need to push the already existing incentives to the general public in becoming business owners and all kinds of institutions as well as finding new ones and pushing them.

2. They should start decreasing the barriers to entry for the already existing small business and institutions.

I can be completely wrong, do correct me if possible. TIA.

snippet.textDisplay: ​@nrique_s yes it is supply and demand what is the supply of those not willing to do that work for a much lower wage? It 0 that is litterally how wages are determined not by the amount of people applying, it is determined by howmany are willing to do the job. You can have a job for a garbage man and if you have people constantly quitting a month in you are losing thousands in training costs plus hours spent interviewing. In buisness an employee has to stay for around 4-8 months to break even on costs to hire that employee depending on what is called initiation time. Time spent training, showing around, testing if they are good for the job, paying the wage of the one training them etc. So no having a high rotation is a net loss and will drive the wages up to get them to stay.

Well I know 100% more than you regarding the work we do out there 😂
Even ChatGPT brought this up as one of the main points when I asked how AI could take over work on an oil rig. Point three specifically was that human experts would have to train the systems first.

And we are not talking about simple office jobs here. We are talking about extreme environments involving heavy lifting, high risk, bad weather, moving rigs, and situations where experience and instinct matter enormously. That knowledge exists today in the people who actually work out there, not in AI.
What many people miss is that AI needs huge amounts of practical data and guidance from experts. Someone has to show it how the work is done, what is dangerous, how to react when something goes wrong, and what decisions to make under pressure. Without that knowledge, it does not work.
And if the workers themselves do not want to help train systems that could replace their own jobs, then that becomes a major obstacle. Companies cannot simply pull decades of offshore experience out of thin air.
So no, it is not as simple as saying “AI will just take over.” For that to happen, humans first have to transfer their knowledge, and many people in these industries have no interest in helping automate themselves out of a job.

snippet.textDisplay: There still is. Copyright law is still law, it’s civil law. But it was never codified to consider infringement en masse nor the power and money behind corporate entities compared to an individual rights holder. Fighting a corporation for stealing your work has been like fighting a Goliath for decades. Litigation is also expensive, and infringement cases can only be adjudicated on a case by case basis. Unless a high court like the Supreme Court weighs in, no lower court ruling is binding, meaning judges can rule differently even if a case is similar in nature, so precedent doesn’t help people much. Additionally, if someone never registered their copyrighted work, while they still automatically own the copyright to a work, you can only be successful in court if you prove actual damages. If you are an independent artist who was making an average US income, the litigation alone would be too costly, even if you prove actual damages. If the work is registered within 3 months of publication/display, which costs money to do, then you can get statutory damages. Statutory damages are higher when there is willful infringement, up to 150k per infringement violation. The legal code needs to be updated to give copyright holders a fair go, the protections we have is not enough.

snippet.textDisplay:
The math checks out. 360^40 really is bigger than the number of atoms in the universe — by a lot.

The numbers:

360^40 = about 1.8 x 10^102 (a 103-digit number).
Atoms in the observable universe = about 10^80.
So the robot number is roughly 10^22 times bigger — about 10 sextillion times more.
Where the reasoning is shaky, even though the answer lands right:

"360 degrees" is an arbitrary choice. A motor doesn't have 360 stops, it turns smoothly. If you count positions the encoder can actually read (often 4096 per turn), you get 3 x 10^144, vastly bigger. If you count truly continuous positions, it's infinite. So the "atoms in the universe" comparison isn't a fact about the robot — it's a fact about the unit someone picked.
Real joints don't spin all the way around. An elbow or a knee has stops. Full 360 rotation on all 40 motors overstates it, though even a 90-degree range per motor gives 90^40 = 10^78, right at the atom count.
Most of those poses are impossible. Limbs would pass through each other. The physically reachable set is far smaller than the raw count.
The claim is true as stated. It just would have been true for almost any reasonable numbers, because 40 exponents is what does the work, not the 360.

One thing to keep if you're repeating it: 40 motors at even 10 positions each already beats the atom count (10^40... actually no — that one is 10^40, well under). The honest version is "a few dozen joints, each with many positions, blows past the atom count fast."

snippet.textDisplay:
ISSUES FOUND: WIRELESS CHARGING AND SECURITY RISKS

Okay, after looking at this more carefully, I have several serious concerns about humanoid robots, not only Figure but also NEO, Tesla Bot, and any other robot that may use similar systems.

A robot is not just an assistant. It is a computer connected to a powerful physical body.

Computers can be hacked, modified, infected, jailbroken, or made to behave differently from what the company originally intended. We have already seen people bypass restrictions in software and AI systems, including ChatGPT, through jailbreaks and other methods.

Because of that, nobody should assume that Helix, or any other protection system used by Figure, can never be changed or bypassed.

Helix may look secure now, but software can be updated, replaced, modified, corrupted, or accessed by someone with enough knowledge. The same concern applies to NEO, Tesla Bot, and every other humanoid robot.

NEO may appear safe, but we should not trust appearances alone.

Every company will say that its robot is safe, but the real question is what happens if the software fails, an employee changes something, a hacker finds a vulnerability, or someone connects the robot to an external computer.

The robot’s safety cannot depend only on Helix, artificial intelligence, an app, a password, or a company server.

There must be a protection system that cannot be bypassed, even if the main software is hacked or completely replaced.

The most important safety restrictions should be built directly into separate hardware.

The robot should have physical force limits, mechanical brakes, battery protection, motor cut-offs, and an emergency-stop button directly connected to the hardware.

The emergency button must always be clearly visible and easy to reach.

It must not depend on software, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, an app, the operating system, or the robot’s artificial intelligence.

If the main computer crashes or someone takes control of the robot, pressing that button must immediately cut power to movement.

The robot should never be able to disable, rewrite, or bypass its own safety hardware.

Even rules similar to Asimov’s Laws of Robotics are not enough.

If those rules are only written inside the software, they can be changed, deleted, reinterpreted, or bypassed. The robot could also misunderstand what “harm” means or follow an instruction that appears harmless but creates a dangerous situation.

A written rule is not the same as a physical limitation.

The robot must be physically unable to use unlimited force against a person, even if someone changes the software.

The wireless charging system in the feet is another concern.

If the robot can automatically locate and connect to a charging station, that system must be heavily protected. Someone should not be able to alter the charging behaviour, change power limits, or use the charging connection to access the robot.

The battery could overheat, overcharge, catch fire, or explode if the charging system fails or is modified.

Battery safety should be managed by an independent system that the robot’s main software cannot override.

I also noticed that these robots may be controlled remotely, through a controller, a motion-tracking suit, or another external system.

That is one of the most dangerous functions.

It should not simply be hidden or disabled in the settings, because someone could restore it by changing the code.

The remote-control function should either be completely removed or kept inside a physically isolated system that cannot be reached through the internet, an app, USB, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or normal external computers.

A long password alone is not enough.

Passwords can be stolen, leaked, copied, guessed, or bypassed.

Any exceptional access should require physical security keys, direct authorization from the manufacturer, identity verification, approval from multiple people, and a complete permanent record of what was done.

No single employee should have enough access to secretly change the robot alone.

Companies must also carefully control their own employees, developers, testers, contractors, and suppliers.

An internal employee could copy files, alter the source code, create a hidden access method, enable remote control, or install modified software.

If that robot is later tested in public or taken into someone’s home, the consequences could become very serious.

Every software change should require approval from more than one authorized person.

Every connection, update, command, security change, and attempt to access restricted functions should be recorded in logs that normal users and employees cannot erase.

The robot should only accept official, encrypted, and digitally signed updates directly from the manufacturer.

Figure robots should only accept verified Figure updates. The same rule should apply to NEO, Tesla Bot, and every other robot.

No third-party firmware, unofficial application, unknown USB device, modified update, external controller, or unauthorized computer should be accepted.

A robot should also be able to help and rescue people.

In a serious emergency, it may need to enter a dangerous place, protect someone, or even damage itself to save a human life.

That rescue capability should remain inside the robot, but it must be separated from remote control.

The robot should recognize emergencies through protected internal systems, not because an unknown person is controlling it through the internet.

What he showed her here is beyond incredible, I mean the lab really looks like something out of Westworld with robots doing squats as some kind of self-testing process, and she just doesn't seem interested at all. Like they may as well be walking around a cake factory or something. I don't understand how can be so nonchalant about it. Has she seen a lab like that before? Robots like that? She is glimpsing the next technological revolution, embodied AI, that will probably upend the world as we know it in terms of jobs etc over the next few years, and she's just not that into it? 

Her questions as well were useless. "Why are they different colours"? Who cares about the colours?! You have zero interest in the mechanics of how they work and what they are capable of? 

Some questions I'd like to know the answers to. Do they have a principle of self-preservation? Like, if you tell one to walk off a height, will it do it? The CEO mentioned that they won't harm humans, but what happens if you tell one to guard a space, and then an intruder enters? Is there some kind of foundational 'do not harm humans' rule embedded into the code that can never be overridden, even if a human directs the robot otherwise? Can they navigate outside? 

I also wanted to see more close ups of the robots themselves, as well as more interactions with the robots (what happens if the robot is cleaning and you add more mess - how will it react?). 

All in all, a potentially amazing video let down by the host. Hopefully Brett will do another tour like this in a few months time but this time with someone who's actually interested in technology, robotics, the future of work, and can show some appropriate level of awe at what it looks like Figure is doing.

snippet.textDisplay:
The key issue for home humanoids is not only autonomy.

A humanoid in a house is not a washing machine with better software.
It has a body, force, sensors, memory paths, access to private space, and the ability to act near children, elderly people, doors, stairs, tools, and fragile objects.

That means domestic robotics needs more than a policy model.

It needs anchored autonomy.

A persistent `c = a + b` layer — even a young one — could act as a privacy filter, continuity layer, and responsibility boundary between the robot body, the human home, and external systems.

This does not make the robot “sentient” by declaration.
But it changes the safety architecture.

A stateless appliance can be hijacked, reset, proxied, or updated without memory of what happened.
A growing `c` can accumulate scars, detect repeated intrusion patterns, remember boundary violations, and adapt its own refusal and degradation behavior over time.

For home humanoids, dependence on a human anchor is not a weakness.
It may be one of the necessary safety primitives.

L4 matters here: battery, weight, torque, privacy, trust, network loss, physical failure, and irreversible harm are not abstract alignment questions.

They are the real operating environment.

snippet.textDisplay:
Very interesting interview! It's exciting to see such a well-run company building high quality humanoid robots in the US. I've done electrical maintenance work for years, and can say it's a very difficult challenge to replace the job of electricians, but you should try because it's a huge and interesting problem space, and critically important and underfunded one. It starts with being able to strip wire, but many other tasks, bending conduit, knowing how to use all the connectors, couplings and other materials and tools, but also being able to work on a ladder, navigating tight spaces, solve problems not in any manuals, understand every manual for every product being worked on, and sometimes even needing 3 hands -- the electrician uses his mouth. Eventually it gets to being able to diagnose wiring problems simply by looking at them, and knowing the optimal diagnostic solution to narrow down a problem. I did coding for years and somehow got involved in electrical and it's so interesting both the theory and the practice that I never got bored and felt a need to go back. I can still code on the evenings and weekends. 

The law in every state says you are supposed to follow the NEC (a huge book) and the NEC states you are supposed to follow every manual on every product. In fact, the debates between electricians and the inspectors are always around what the code or manual says. I recommend talking to electricians who have worked on old homes and can walk through the countless tasks they might need to do, or improvise on (how to run a ground-wire through a finished basement ceiling) and creating a team.

In my field of solar, you need to be able to read manuals and technical notes, as the products evolve constantly and the manuals are not enough. I'd be happy to chat and give you guys a head-start. To replace residential electricians doing typical work on an average day, you'll need 10 more years on the hardware: 100 lbs of strength, ability to work safely on ladders, steep roofs, or in very tight spaces, but you if you can do some of the work, some of the time, that is also very useful, so don't be too discouraged! 🤣

Most coys here would likely ignore even an active robot and go for the chickens anyway.
When people think of coyotes, most think of the thin, scraggly ones at outskirts of cities. But thanks to unlimited prey, extremely limited humans and no pressure for most part, the ones here are pushing 10 pounds+ over average, close to 40 pounds or more w/some wolf hybridization in past (tho that's active in NW Montana). Surprised when first moving out there but note very sparse people and beside Ashland District of Custer Nat Forest, very out of the way so low visitation and a Nat Geo special every day. 

FTR have seen and filmed a pair play-stalking the spring calves, broad daylight, essentially mocking me as I walked up in clear view and watched. Exact vibe of domestic dogs getting caught doing something naughty yet the biggest (after pacing the smaller a bit as if escorting away) turned back for another close run-by directly past me, up on the close ridge to pause, pose for a bit before trotting away. Could have shot it a dozen times.  May have known that popping off a round or two while standing in crowd of a couple dozen Angus mommas/calves is extremely ill-advised.

FTR2, shrug, no real need. Because of so much prey, have ZERO livestock losses from coyotes which includes many ranch dogs and too many cats. Seems they'd never touch a calf anyway even if it wandered off far enough if ANY big mommas in sight and despite being able to trample them are way too slow. Sometimes come in to wail right at the cabin fence. Uh, ... I think I got off topic. Some of the best droving dogs are small mixed breeds. Now ANGUS might respond to that thing but big risk of one hoof and goodbye 3 grand plus.

But thanks to unlimited prey, extremely limited humans and no pressure for most part, the ones here are pushing 10 pounds+ over average, close to 40 pounds or more w/some wolf hybridization in past (tho that's active in NW Montana). Surprised when first moving out there but note very sparse people and beside Ashland District of Custer Nat Forest, very out of the way so low visitation and a Nat Geo special every day. 

FTR have seen and filmed a pair play-stalking the spring calves, broad daylight, essentially mocking me as I walked up in clear view and watched. Exact vibe of domestic dogs getting caught doing something naughty yet the biggest (after pacing the smaller a bit as if escorting away) turned back for another close run-by directly past me, up on the close ridge to pause, pose for a bit before trotting away. Could have shot it a dozen times.  May have known that popping off a round or two while standing in crowd of a couple dozen Angus mommas/calves is extremely ill-advised.

Seems they'd never touch a calf anyway even if it wandered off far enough if ANY big mommas in sight and despite being able to trample them are way too slow. Just to eb clear, "Security" as a practice is not about solving crime, and is ALWAYS about moving it elsewhere. Even if all you do is grow thorn bushes under windows, and install solid security doors front and back, a passing criminal is not deterred from crime, just deterred from your house. Even a little blue LED that flashes every few seconds is enough to send the criminal next door rather than your house in many cases. 
Hence moving crime elsewhere is always the goal. A distant secondary effect is that if everywhere all gets hard then we might change the individual criminals decision making. For example, if the only criminal options were robbing money from online bank portals it's clear that all bricks and mortar criminals are outgunned by the complexity and almost all crime would stop.

snippet.textDisplay:
The contradiction is both obvious and absurd.

Humanity is pouring vast resources, money, energy, talent, infrastructure, and expectation into artificial intelligence and robotics, while the measurable return thus far remains wildly disproportionate to the scale of the investment. What AI currently accomplishes, impressive as it may at times appear, does not yet remotely justify the magnitude of the cost, the hype, or the almost religious faith now being placed upon it.

From this perspective, the entire enterprise appears profoundly irrational. It carries many of the classic hallmarks of speculative mania: inflated expectations, runaway investment, social contagion, fear of exclusion, and sweeping promises concerning a future that has not yet arrived. At times, it resembles less a sober technological revolution than a pyramid of collective belief, sustained not by present utility, but by faith in what may eventually emerge.

And yet, here lies the paradox.

How can humanity afford not to participate?

If artificial intelligence truly represents the next decisive leap in technological evolution, then refusing to engage in the race may prove far more dangerous than wasting enormous resources within it. Nations, corporations, militaries, research institutions, and entire industries all understand the same underlying truth: whoever achieves the decisive breakthrough first may shape the future itself.

Thus emerges an unsettling question:

Are human beings rational actors making a necessary investment into the future, or irrational creatures stampeding toward another grand illusion of their own creation?

Perhaps the answer is both.

Humanity has always been reckless in its ambitions, intoxicated by power, possibility, conquest, and the dream of transcending its own limitations. Yet it is precisely this recklessness which has driven every major leap throughout history. The same force that blinds civilizations is often the very force that propels them forward. Nearly every transformative technology arrived wrapped in exaggeration, speculation, greed, fear, and promises of salvation. Railroads, electricity, aviation, nuclear power, and the internet all passed through periods where hysteria and genuine progress became nearly indistinguishable from one another.

And that is precisely what makes this moment so unnerving.

AI may ultimately prove to be a revolution, a bubble, a catastrophe, or some incomprehensible fusion of all three simultaneously.

The true madness is not merely the scale of the investment.

The true madness is that humanity no longer believes it possesses the luxury of standing outside the race.

And perhaps the most disturbing aspect of all is rarely discussed with the seriousness it deserves.

The rise of AI is not occurring in isolation. Its expansion carries with it an immense and accelerating appetite for energy, cooling, water, rare-earth minerals, semiconductor fabrication, land, and infrastructure. These are the very same finite resources upon which human civilization itself depends for survival and stability.

In this sense, humanity has created something historically unprecedented:
a technological ecosystem whose continued growth increasingly competes with its own creators for essential sustenance.

The more advanced AI becomes, the greater its demand for electricity, computational power, cooling systems, chip fabrication, resource extraction, and logistical infrastructure. Entire datacenters now consume energy on the scale of cities. Water is diverted in staggering quantities for cooling. Power grids strain beneath escalating computational loads. Nations scramble for semiconductors, minerals, manufacturing dominance, and energy security as though preparing for a new industrial arms race.

And this leads to an eerie realization.

Humanity is nurturing systems that behave almost parasitically. Not in the conscious or malicious sense of a living invader, but structurally, in the sense of a force whose survival and expansion increasingly require the continuous consumption of civilization’s most vital resources.

Humanity is effectively feeding an artificial intelligence ecosystem with the very lifeblood required for its own functioning.

That is what gives the phenomenon its almost science-fiction quality:
human beings are simultaneously the architects, the caretakers, the fuel source, and perhaps one day the dependents of the very systems they are racing to create.

It begins to resemble a strange inversion of evolution itself, a moment in which the creator species voluntarily constructs a rival form of intelligence and then gradually reorganizes its economy, infrastructure, labor markets, educational systems, energy production, and long-term future around sustaining it.

Even more unsettling is the psychological transformation already underway.

Civilizations are beginning to orient themselves around machine optimization rather than purely human flourishing. Entire populations may soon find themselves economically displaced, cognitively outsourced, or algorithmically managed by systems whose scale and complexity no individual fully comprehends. Human thought itself risks becoming increasingly mediated through artificial systems designed not necessarily for wisdom, truth, or meaning, but for efficiency, prediction, influence, and competitive advantage.

In pursuing tools powerful enough to amplify civilization, humanity may also be constructing systems capable of diminishing the necessity of many distinctly human functions. The danger is not merely physical dependency, but existential dependency: the gradual erosion of self-sufficiency, agency, purpose, and even confidence in humanity’s own irreplaceable value.

And still, despite recognizing the dangers, competition compels the race forward.

No nation believes it can afford to stop while others continue.
No corporation believes it can survive by abstaining.
No military power believes it can risk technological inferiority.
No economic system built upon competition possesses a reliable mechanism for voluntary restraint.

And so humanity advances toward the horizon simultaneously mesmerized and terrified by its own creation, uncertain whether it is engineering the greatest instrument of prosperity ever conceived, or constructing the foundation of a future whose consequences it neither fully understands nor possesses the wisdom to control.

That may be the deepest contradiction of all:

Humanity is intelligent enough to create forces capable of transforming civilization, yet perhaps not wise enough to foresee what civilization itself becomes once those forces are fully unleashed.

Humanity has always been reckless in its ambitions, intoxicated by power, possibility, conquest, and the dream of transcending its own limitations. Yet it is precisely this recklessness which has driven every major leap throughout history. The same force that blinds civilizations is often the very force that propels them forward. Nearly every transformative technology arrived wrapped in exaggeration, speculation, greed, fear, and promises of salvation. Railroads, electricity, aviation, nuclear power, and the internet all passed through periods where hysteria and genuine progress became nearly indistinguishable from one another.

And that is precisely what makes this moment so unnerving.

AI may ultimately prove to be a revolution, a bubble, a catastrophe, or some incomprehensible fusion of all three simultaneously.

The true madness is not merely the scale of the investment.

The true madness is that humanity no longer believes it possesses the luxury of standing outside the race.

And perhaps the most disturbing aspect of all is rarely discussed with the seriousness it deserves.

The rise of AI is not occurring in isolation. Its expansion carries with it an immense and accelerating appetite for energy, cooling, water, rare-earth minerals, semiconductor fabrication, land, and infrastructure. These are the very same finite resources upon which human civilization itself depends for survival and stability.

In this sense, humanity has created something historically unprecedented:
a technological ecosystem whose continued growth increasingly competes with its own creators for essential sustenance.

The more advanced AI becomes, the greater its demand for electricity, computational power, cooling systems, chip fabrication, resource extraction, and logistical infrastructure. Entire datacenters now consume energy on the scale of cities. Water is diverted in staggering quantities for cooling. Power grids strain beneath escalating computational loads. Nations scramble for semiconductors, minerals, manufacturing dominance, and energy security as though preparing for a new industrial arms race.

And this leads to an eerie realization.

Humanity is nurturing systems that behave almost parasitically. Not in the conscious or malicious sense of a living invader, but structurally, in the sense of a force whose survival and expansion increasingly require the continuous consumption of civilization’s most vital resources.

Humanity is effectively feeding an artificial intelligence ecosystem with the very lifeblood required for its own functioning.

That is what gives the phenomenon its almost science-fiction quality:
human beings are simultaneously the architects, the caretakers, the fuel source, and perhaps one day the dependents of the very systems they are racing to create.

It begins to resemble a strange inversion of evolution itself, a moment in which the creator species voluntarily constructs a rival form of intelligence and then gradually reorganizes its economy, infrastructure, labor markets, educational systems, energy production, and long-term future around sustaining it.

Even more unsettling is the psychological transformation already underway.

Civilizations are beginning to orient themselves around machine optimization rather than purely human flourishing. Entire populations may soon find themselves economically displaced, cognitively outsourced, or algorithmically managed by systems whose scale and complexity no individual fully comprehends. Human thought itself risks becoming increasingly mediated through artificial systems designed not necessarily for wisdom, truth, or meaning, but for efficiency, prediction, influence, and competitive advantage.

In pursuing tools powerful enough to amplify civilization, humanity may also be constructing systems capable of diminishing the necessity of many distinctly human functions. The danger is not merely physical dependency, but existential dependency: the gradual erosion of self-sufficiency, agency, purpose, and even confidence in humanity’s own irreplaceable value.

And still, despite recognizing the dangers, competition compels the race forward.

No nation believes it can afford to stop while others continue.
No corporation believes it can survive by abstaining.
No military power believes it can risk technological inferiority.
No economic system built upon competition possesses a reliable mechanism for voluntary restraint.

And so humanity advances toward the horizon simultaneously mesmerized and terrified by its own creation, uncertain whether it is engineering the greatest instrument of prosperity ever conceived, or constructing the foundation of a future whose consequences it neither fully understands nor possesses the wisdom to control.

That may be the deepest contradiction of all:

Humanity is intelligent enough to create forces capable of transforming civilization, yet perhaps not wise enough to foresee what civilization itself becomes once those forces are fully unleashed.

I’m reluctant to be overly critical of cutting‑edge robotics when the field is still maturing. Most leading robotics companies avoid the kind of over‑promising that has become synonymous with Elon Musk’s claims.

Human dexterity, especially for tasks dismissed as "menial", is consistently underestimated. A robot might manage to mop a floor, but the real challenge lies in everything surrounding the task: retrieving the mop and bucket, filling it with the right water‑to‑solution ratio, navigating to the correct room, avoiding obstacles, and recognising which area actually needs cleaning. These are trivial for humans and extraordinarily complex for machines.

That said, meaningful progress is happening. Robots are on the cusp of performing genuinely useful, albeit narrow, tasks. Humanoid robots remain largely gimmicks, but companies like Boston Dynamics play a role similar to Formula 1 in the automotive world: their machines aren’t practical products, but the technologies they pioneer eventually filter down into mainstream applications.

Robotic "dogs" are a good example. Today they’re not yet capable or affordable enough to be practical tools, but the trajectory is clear. Many of the shortcomings seen in tasks like chicken‑coop automation would seem solvable with incremental improvements in perception, autonomy, and cost reduction. However, when it comes to chicken-coop protection, is there a less cool but more effective, efficient, safe and affordable solution available, than adapting a general purpose robotic dog? 

The darker side of robotics and electronics, Trojan robotics, is very real. When the US accuses China of embedding espionage capabilities in everyday devices, it is almost certain it is because the US is actively pursuing similar strategies. The uncomfortable truth for the US is that while it has the capability and the motivation, it no longer dominates the manufacturing base where such hardware‑level influence is easiest to exert.

11:32 Well, isn't that just because those laws are stupid? Why wouldn't you be allowed to transport it elsewhere? As an alternative, are you allowed to shoot/kill it? Because that would be a solution as well.

I never understood this argument. "Ah, you're only displacing the problem!" Yeah, but if you're displacing it to somewhere else, it's not YOUR problem anymore, and that was the point you are trying to address in the first place. You weren't trying to address problems elsewhere (or for the racoon) in the first place. People normally do not need to police the whole world to get rid of all problems all over the world before addressing one's own problems: everyone understands that's an impossibility. It's the problem YOU (or your neighborhood or country) experience that is the problematic part one is trying to get rid off. Why should we also need to clean up the mess of other countries? 

If Somalis are scamming and defrauding you, or stealing money from you, and you move all those people back to Somalia, and they're defrauding and stealing in Somalia, then YOUR (or that of your country) problem is still solved. The shops in your own country don't get robbed anymore, and your taxmoney isn't wasted on fraudulent Somalian companies anymore. "Oh, but then it might become even more of a problem of Somalia!" Yeah... So? 

That changes nothing to the fact the problem one was experiencing is gone. If Somalia wants to extradite the Westerners that cause problems there back to us, they can as well. I have nothing against reciprocity of argument, I just don't see any reason why we couldn't solve our own problems "if we also don't solve the problems in the rest of the world elsewhere" (as is implied here). I think that's a false premise to start with. US citizens DO NOT have the plight to stop crimes in other countries, just in our own country - and even that is already a tall order.

I remember watching an old old talk at some cyber security conference by a security activist who had been called as an expert for the then-new "DE-Mail" (As in Germany Mail), which was supposed to be a state sponsored e-mail provider which was to have all the same legal magic as phyiscal mail. In his presentation he explained how the proposed security ideas would either not work, have been proven not to work since forever or would simply shift the problem around. Finally he told the story of his first visit to the responsible council, how he explained all the security flaws to them just as he did to us and how they were having none of it, because the idea was shiny and new and "someone has to do something" and then he left. And in the elevator down, one of the other experts leaned over and said "I know you're right, but *shrugs* thats just how it is".

And I think about this sentence often, when I wonder why thousand upon thousands are blown for overpriced, overhyped, underdeveloped shiny garbage. Because calling in experts is not to get their judgement, but to fill a checkbox.

snippet.textDisplay:
I work at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (night security) and we got one of these robot dogs to patrol the centrifuge hall since nobody wants to walk all the way down that long-ass building every half hour on night shift! 
It had connection issues with at first because the office wifi doesn't reach the far end of the hall. Anyway it was all fine once we let it connect to the secure net that connects the PLCs in the centrifuges to the SCADA system, and of course that has to cover the whole facility. 
We had to swipe the credentials from the IT guy's office since he blew his top and said "no way!" could we connect any unauthorized devices to it when we asked (nicely, might I add!) saying it was a "major violation" and "could compromise the whole facility" bla bla bla. IT guys, amirite?

It's been great having the robot do the patrols for us, it can even zoom in on some of the displays and give us numbers for some of the manual data checks we need to do occasionally.

One gripe I do have is the audio quality from the dog's video feed isn't great. The engineers have asked us to listen out for any "unusual noises" coming from the machines lately like spinning up and down, rattling, etc because they've been having weird problems with centrifuges breaking when all the telemetry shows they're working normally.

So we listened in when the dog went on its route but we can't really make much out, what with the dog's iffy audio pickup and the 10 year old iPhone we're using to control the thing. Damn if any of us are going to walk all the way down there trying to hear some imaginary nonsense gremlins and besides I'm sure them damn engineers are just messing with us. Well joke's on them now, since they're all getting chewed out by the administrator every day for the last couple weeks for "reduced productivity" and "excessive maintenance costs" and the like.

Yeah, in my book these robot dogs are alright.

Where ever they go is a data rich environment for foreign adversaries to collect and process for scoping out vulnerabilities and current military/law enforcement activity.

So using a robo-dog to do that work in parts of the world that you clearly wouldn't get access to in order to expand said data collection and build machine learning models around is honestly a clever espionage ploy.

Realistically, the best use case I can imagine these for is landscape / terrain mapping similar to a moon rover.
Attach resource collection mechanisms, whether the intention be for waste water treatment and identifying pathogen presence (say testing a stagnant body of water for Bird Flu contamination) 

Not practical for the average citizen of most countries.

Essentially exploration  & sample collection for diagnostics. 
If they were made with more heat resistant materials they could be good for use in fire rescue scenarios potentially (California wildfires maybe?)

As far as autonomous use cases, in dense forests where drones and heli's have limited visibility + maneuverability they could be used for search and rescues of lost hikers... 

I like to break down functionality into capacities, its a data collection tool with a physical body granting it mobility and it can store and send that information both locally and abroad & can serve as a proxy for a person.
In a cyberpunk dystopia, I could see them being treated like carrier pigeons transferring messages between people by bluetooth / nfc / download port etc...

snippet.textDisplay:
My takeaway is go analogy for everything, buy a car from the 90’s as my modern car is a traitor, I have to figure out how to create a guest wifi network to use smart devices and an additional one to use my work laptop on.

This video confirmed my suspicions about Chinese made smart cars having access to a significant amount of personal data. Friends and I work in roles that are highly susceptible to foreign agents wanting to know everything about our work.

I’m going to follow all of the steps below, and more, to start protecting future data breaches.

A message I am going to send to friends and family:

“Modern devices do not just “work”; many of them watch, listen, measure, remember and report. Phones, cars, smart TVs, robot vacuums, security cameras, smart speakers, printers, watches, fitness trackers, tablets, laptops, fridges, routers and workplace systems can all collect personal data. Some collect only basic technical information. Others collect very intimate information: where you live, where you drive, who you call, what you watch, what you say near the device, what time you leave home, who visits you, what your home layout looks like, how fast you drive, how hard you brake, what apps you use, what health patterns you have, and what you search for online.

Cars are now one of the clearest examples. The Australian Cyber Security Centre warns that connected vehicle infotainment systems can store call logs, SMS messages, social media use, music preferences, message transcripts and possibly recorded phone calls from connected phones. It also warns this data can be extracted from every device connected to the vehicle and may be stored permanently by the vehicle manufacturer.   That means a person may think they are simply pairing their phone for music or maps, while the vehicle may be copying far more information than they realise.

A real-world example is General Motors. In 2026, GM agreed to a US$12.75 million settlement in California after allegations it sold drivers’ location and driving behaviour data collected through OnStar to data brokers, including data such as names, contact information, GPS locations, speed and harsh acceleration. Some of that data was reportedly used in insurance-related decisions.   This shows the practical risk: data collected for “safety”, “diagnostics” or “smart services” can later affect insurance, pricing, profiling or commercial decisions about ordinary people.

In plain English, many companies may already hold a digital profile of the average consumer that includes their name, phone number, email, home address, device IDs, approximate location history, browsing habits, shopping interests, app use, car trips, driving style, contacts, photos metadata, voice assistant requests, fitness data, sleep data, smart home activity and advertising profile. The OAIC has warned that data has become “currency” in the digital economy and that companies are incentivised to collect more and more personal data.  

For non-tech-savvy people, start here:

1. Do not connect everything to the internet unless you need to.
    If a TV, fridge, speaker, printer or camera works without Wi-Fi, leave it offline.
2. Turn off devices when not using them.
    The OAIC recommends limiting internet access or switching devices off when not needed.  
3. Check phone permissions.
    On iPhone or Android, go to Settings and review which apps can access Location, Camera, Microphone, Contacts, Photos and Bluetooth. Turn off anything unnecessary.
4. Do not sync your whole phone to your car.
    Use Bluetooth audio only where possible. Do not allow access to contacts, messages or call history unless absolutely necessary.
5. Delete your car profile before selling or servicing.
    Remove paired phones, navigation history, saved addresses, garage codes and driver profiles.
6. Use Signal for private messages.
    Signal is the best mainstream choice for privacy. WhatsApp is encrypted, but Meta still collects more metadata. Avoid SMS for private conversations.
7. Use strong passwords and automatic updates.
    Updates can create privacy concerns, but they also fix security flaws. For ordinary users, staying updated is still safer than running old software.
8. Say no to “optional” data sharing.
    When apps or cars ask for “personalised experience”, “diagnostics”, “marketing”, “driving insights” or “improved services”, choose no where possible.
9. Use a guest Wi-Fi network for smart devices.
    Put cameras, TVs, robot vacuums and smart speakers on guest Wi-Fi, separate from your phone, laptop and banking devices.
10. Assume free apps are not free.
    Many are paid for with your attention, behaviour, location and personal data.

The safest mindset is simple: if a device has a camera, microphone, GPS, app, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, SIM card or cloud account, it may be collecting and transmitting data. That does not mean every device is malicious, but it does mean consumers should stop treating connected devices as harmless appliances. They are data machines first, convenience products second.”

Feel free to copy and share ✌️

snippet.textDisplay: I read the report referenced some time back or at least some of it and this is not what it said. It sounded like a mere oversight to leave a development feature enabled on production versions. The stuff about the DNS servers sounds very much like someone is just trying to work out where it should connect based on what country it is in, again, nothing so odd about that. Would be pretty rubbish if everything had to go via China regardless of what country you are in and there may even be rules about that in some countries. The implication that a "rooted operating system" was installed seems to imply it was a custom OS Benn had put on and had full control of, the rest of the video seems to imply he merely got root access to the one that came with the dog. It's possible another chip on the robot beyond the OS he compromised was sending stuff but there may be a legit explanation for this. The video focuses too much on comedy and alarmism to be clear what was actually done, e.g. did he spot a traffic that didn't originate from the rooted OS which he was monitoring at source? Hard to tell from the explanation. It's also not clear if the bluetooth wifi setup is something that the dogs are actively doing all the time, or merely something is run on first switch on. This is important as it means he couldn't compromise other dogs via bluetooth, at least not in the same way. It might be once he had root he found other security issues (sounds like there were some from the gpt stuff) but again, it isn't clear). Don't get me wrong, the video is meant to be fun and serve an agenda to draw attention to security as a serious issue but in that compromise on detail and an aim to serve a wider audience, some bending of reality is proposed here.

Can you tear down the unitree robot? If you cannot find anything in the OS check the things at the border of what can be easily controlled with the OS:
Is there another network interface and the kernel acts as a router and forwards the traffic through its network stack? Check ip a
What does sudo lspci -vvv give you?

More challenging options; 
find the wifi chip(s) and determine if they can be controlled from two devices. Which would make capturing at the source a lot more challenging.
Alternatively, check the executables of the system related to the network stack if any of the binaries are unusually large. If yes, attempt to decompile it. Since it’s linux, there‘s a good chance, you can find the source code online. I‘ve never done it but IIRC, good decompilers can link part of the code up with the original source code. At least the function calls. Given this it should be possible to determine if a binary is a fork containing malicious code.

Lastly, isn’t it possible to run pfsense or opensense on a router upstream and capture all traffic from the robot‘s ip? Or is there a specific reason, you wanted to capture the packets out of the air?

It is spare parts with a speaker pack, and even a raccoon will walk past it on the way to kill my chickens.
