snippet.textDisplay:
You are angry that the government will not let you hurt a raccoon to protect your chickens.

But stop for one second.

You want to hurt the raccoon so you can keep the chickens alive long enough to hurt them yourself later.

So what is this really about?

It is not about protecting life.
It is about protecting property.

The government is not morally clean either. It does not truly protect animals. It protects legal categories. The raccoon is “wildlife.” The chicken is “livestock.” One is regulated. The other is owned. That is not morality. That is paperwork.

But you are not morally clean either if your argument is: “I should be allowed to kill this animal because it threatens the animals I plan to use.”

So the ugly truth is this:

The government is not defending life.
You are not defending life.
Both sides are defending control.

The state wants control over violence.
You want control over your property.
And the animals are trapped inside both systems.

So before you ask, “Why won’t they let me kill the raccoon?” ask the harder question:

Why do you think your convenience gives you the right to decide which living being deserves protection and which one becomes a product?

snippet.textDisplay:
Most layer 3 switches have a feature called "port mirroring" - that will allow you to copy any traffic on one port to another port. You can use this to sniff raw packets without either side knowing. Note, this is not _wireless_ traffic.
You can also do something similar with a HUB (ie: non-switching ethernet hub) as they forward all packets to all ports by default.

snippet.textDisplay:
One thing I feel I should point out is that your quick math on the cost of a security guard ignores some very important, and expensive, nuance around hiring employees. Please note that I personally still think a human living in the US, preferably in the same city as the monitored property, should be involved regardless of the tech. Cool new tech does not HAVE to displace US workers, it CAN be done well. 

Back to the cost though.  The better quick math is to take the employee salary and double it. Google says Atlanta pays security guards about 40k (plus or minus 5k) per year. So at a minimum, the company cost is roughly 80k per year, which is $6,666 per month. You double it because of the plethora of expenses that come with every employee above their base salary. Employer share of taxes, unemployment insurance premiums, workers comp insurance, paid sick leave, paid vacation, 401K, medical insurance, reimbursed expenses (mileage, meals, travel), training, certifications, and a few other odds and ends. Even part time has plenty of extra costs and potential costs. And that’s just your run of the mill office worker. For security guards I’m sure there is also additional insurance and certification costs related to the use of force and carrying weapons in some cases. And on top of all of that, the cost of finding a new employee is not trivial. And on top of that, the cost of managing an employee is not trivial. And on top of that, the potential cost of firing an employee and enduring a legal battle might not be trivial. And if you just hire a security company you’ll have a “flat” rate of some kind, but that will certainly be even more than the employee cost because the security firm would mark all of that up to turn a profit of course. 

So no, a security guard does not only cost $3,000 per month. I’m not saying these dogs are wonderful, I’m just saying that the economics do make a ton of sense at that price point. Especially if the contract has some flexibility that allows for quickly increasing or reducing the number of units by a certain amount without a contract modification. I could easily see a contract like this have a minimum of say 10 units, but allow for increasing to 20 and reducing back to 10 over a certain timeframe. That would allow for seasonal changes and special events and things like that. Could be MUCH easier than hiring on even a temp security guard for a weekend event.

Secondly, the main reason, is the king cobra situation. In the times of the British Raj the British wanted to get rid of king cobras that were in lots of places in India in that time, so they came up with the idea of paying poor Indians to bring them the decapitated heads of king cobras assuming that they would kill any snake they see and then gladly go collect the bounty. They didn't, what they decided to do was start breeding king cobras en masse and eventually some of the now massive amounts of cobras got out into the wild and bred with wild cobras and eventually they ended up with more cobras in the wild than before the policy.

If we pay homeless people, by giving them a house, then all we do is effectively invite in more homeless people who will demand another house. snippet.textDisplay:
@3nertia Money is as real as systems of socioeconomics (like communism and capitolism) because people inherently place values on commodities, finished goods, and services. Because different people in different areas value things differently (shocker, I know), this creates a need for systems of exchange between groups. As networks of exchange become increasingly large and complex, having a form of currency is necessary. Sometimes the currency is in the form of valuable commodities, such as gold and silver made into coins, or valuable food sources like rice. But it's often observed that carrying around large amounts of heavy metals or grains to trade with is inconvenient, so when trust is high it is easier to use representational currency that can be exchanged for the promise of physical goods with an agreed upon value. Examples include rai stones and wampum shells. And as the power of centralized governments grows, they can leverage their power and resources to back the valuation of fiat currencies, which have no intrinsic value but gain extrinsic value from the backing of large, stable, established centralized national governments. 

So money is real, as real as other ideas like morals and politics and systems of economic exchange. You can't hold any of these things in your hands, but they arise from our human nature, from our natural set of evolved behaviors which we find to be common among members of our species.

“I am afraid the ordinary citizen will not like to be told that the banks can, and do, create money…. And they who control the credit of the nation direct the policy of Governments and hold in the hollow of their hands the destiny of the people.”
— Carroll Quigley, Tragedy and Hope 

“The powers of financial capitalism had another far-reaching aim, nothing less than to create a world system of financial control in private hands able to dominate the political system of each country and the economy of the world as a whole. This system was to be controlled in a feudalistic fashion by the central banks of the world acting in concert, by secret agreements arrived at in frequent meetings and conferences. The apex of the system was to be the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, Switzerland, a private bank owned and controlled by the world's central banks which were themselves private corporations. Each central bank...sought to dominate its government by its ability to control Treasury loans, to manipulate foreign exchanges, to influence the level of economic activity in the country, and to influence cooperative politicians by subsequent economic rewards in the business world.”
— Carroll Quigley, Tragedy and Hope: A History of the World in Our Time

“For the first time in its history, Western Civilization is in danger of being destroyed internally by a corrupt, criminal ruling cabal which is centered around the Rockefeller interests, which include elements from the Morgan, Brown, Rothschild, Du Pont, Harriman, Kuhn-Loeb, and other groupings as well. This junta took control of the political, financial, and cultural life of America in the first two decades of the twentieth century.”
— Carroll Quigley, Tragedy and Hope 

“In effect, this creation of paper claims greater than the reserves available means that bankers were creating money out of nothing. The same thing could be done in another way, not by note-issuing banks but by deposit banks. Deposit bankers discovered that orders and checks drawn against deposits by depositors and given to third persons were often not cashed by the latter but were deposited to their own accounts. Thus there were no actual movements of funds, and payments were made simply by bookkeeping transactions on the accounts. Accordingly, it was necessary for the banker to keep on hand in actual money … no more than the fraction of deposits likely to be drawn upon and cashed; the rest could be used for loans, and if these loans were made by creating a deposit for the borrower, who in turn would draw checks upon it rather than withdraw it in money, such ‘created deposits’ or loans could also be covered adequately by retaining reserves to only a fraction of their value.”
— Carroll Quigley, Tragedy and Hope 


“The argument that the two parties should represent opposed ideals and policies, one, perhaps, of the Right and the other of the Left, is a foolish idea acceptable only to doctrinaire and academic thinkers. Instead, the two parties should be almost identical, so that the American people can ‘throw the rascals out’ at any election without leading to any profound or extensive shifts in policy. … Either party in office becomes in time corrupt, tired, unenterprising, and vigorless. Then it should be possible to replace it, every four years if necessary, by the other party, which will be none of these things but will still pursue, with new vigor, approximately the same basic policies.”
— Carroll Quigley, Tragedy and Hope 

“There does exist, and has existed for a generation, an international Anglophile network which operates, to some extent, in the way the radical Right believes the Communists act. In fact, this network, which we may identify as the Round Table Groups, has no aversion to cooperating with the Communists, or any other groups, and frequently does so. I know of the operations of this network because I have studied it for twenty years and was permitted for two years, in the early 1960's, to examine its papers and secret records. I have no aversion to it or to most of its aims and have, for much of my life, been close to it and to many of its instruments. I have objected, both in the past and recently, to a few of its policies [...], but in general my chief difference of opinion is that it wishes to remain unknown, and I believe its role in history is significant enough to be known.”
— Carroll Quigley, Tragedy and Hope

I think a lot of these fancy slick shiny robot toys are something I've taken to calling Tautological Technologies.

They're not technologies being developed and deployed to solve real issues faced by real people in real life. They're being developed and deployed because they're just What The Future Looks Like.

Silicon Valley is a place with a million and one unoriginal ideas. For all the big tech wankoff about ~Innovation~, their most successful tactic is just ripping off science fiction from the last century and patting themselves on the back for it.

I think this is especially true of humanoid robots. There's very few use cases for humanoid robots that aren't just Human Shaped Servant I Don't Have To Feel Bad About, but billions of dollars keep getting invested in humanoid robots because they're Futuristic. And we know they're in the future because they're in all those Future Movies.

I think this is a lot of Silicon Valley right now. Silicon Valley is populated primarily by dudes who think movies are real. Why are humanoid robots, AI, the cybertruck, stainless rockets, etc. The Future? Because the movies said so. And movies are real.

I believe that you can tell the truth of this by how not one single Tech Innovator who's gotten on stage in the last fifteen years seems like he'd know the first thing about a Buckminster Fullerene. But he absolutely has strong opinions on the forty-eight different cuts of Blade Runner.

As a note, foxes actually prefer the eggs.  They end up eating the hens because the hens often get killed defending the eggs, so the fox runs off with the hen's body to eat as well, because waste not want that.

As of the malware, I have a sneaking suspicion it is possibly in the embedded system, not in the firmware.  

Additionally, it may or may not be uploading anything substantial,.  It could be just phoning home so the manufacturer can measure deployment of their products.  Still, it is quite nasty that the board won't activate without the initial DNS checks passing.  This means China could kill these robodogs by simply killing those DNS servers, or otherwise altering them to appear funny to it.

Additionally, even if this isn't intended as advanced malware, it may accidentally open backdoors as so many such test and phone home routines have the potential for exploits, and if it is in low level firmware one could gain sub-root access through them enabling potential invisible malware to be installed.

couple of things;

- DNS is used to confirm general internet connectivity all the time
- picking your DNS server based on location is also normal. Why make DNS requests to china if the device is in USA?
- defaulting to calling it "malware" when you have 0 information that the behaviour is malicious is just straight up incorrect. Suspicious, sure. but you cannot just call it malware because you don't know what it's doing.
- calling it some of the most advanced malware you've seen is sincerely laughable. Every piece of chinese technology ever is basically infamous for phoning home. What about this is advanced, other than your general lack of exposure to malware?
- Using "encrypted handshake" like its some big deal when that's literally just any TCP connection... aka all session-based connectivity. That's just how the internet works. It doesn't make the traffic somehow super secret.

You went through all this effort - why not implement SSL decrypt in-line and see what's actually going on?

Your intent to educate and inform on cybersecurity is commendable, but there is many things in here bordering on misinformation. there is more than enough FUD going around for real issues - this is essentially a non-discovery until you dig deeper.

I worked with professional sewer scanning LIDAR systems about 15 years ago.  Specifically, I was just replacing the motors, but the point here is that they were environmentally sealed in a gas-proof cylinder, with what I believe was a quartz ring about 1 inch wide around it near the top, for the laser to shine through. 

There's no good excuse for leaving the gimbals/cores on a high-movement precision device exposed like that... Unless you WANT it to fail quickly, requiring expensive repairs.

snippet.textDisplay:
​​@msytdc1577 No, but you do get there by using a part that costs $22 but putting $899 on the BOL. 
I DO know the production costs. That's what I did. Built equipment for government agencies/military hardware. Yea, the stuff with the 0.2 micron tolerance.  Ugh. 

So yeah... I stand by my assessment.  
Making the most critical, most sensitive, easily damaged piece hang down by the ground, unshielded, is a deliberate design choice. It's meant to fail. 

I've seen both sides... let's just say I don't respect the EPA and their spending the way most do. 
I know what they pay and what they claim they paid.
The only thing I don't know is WHOSE pockets 85-90% of the money is going into. It's not the vendor/manufacturing shop...

Edit : what I'm saying is that both this company AND Boston Dynamics are far, far overpricing, but BD gets away with it by being the first/doing actual research and development. 
They need to make back the investment. They're just... Excessively aggressive, it would seem. 

These copycat knock-off companies though... Its just pure profit. 
Use the cheapest parts available that TECHNICALLY qualify as "the same thing" and sell $1200 hardware for $3600, making small changes to render it less reliable, knowing it'll be back for service every 2-4 months, guaranteeing a constant $1200 per fix cycle of repairs.  (But hey, that's still cheaper than buying a new one, right? ... is what they'll say about it for the first year.) 

Also... I've built 2 systems using sealed LIDAR as described above. Mine were slightly slower, but otherwise the same. (And that comes down to my custom control board/personal code skill. I'm aware it could do better.) 

They cost me around $90USD each. Submersible, acid/gasproof. No control board etc but the point is sealing a lidar module raises the price from around $60 to $90USD - and they're still working over a decade later. Outside. Direct weather exposure... to the outside of the modules. 
The only problems they've ever had were easily rectified with a damp cloth. (Mud over the lens LOL)

Sooo... no good excuse at that price level still.
It's all about the 10000% roi on repairs. 

I can smell planned obsolescence from a production mile away. I'm THAT kind of obnoxious engineer who asks "... But why?"

snippet.textDisplay:
@mrbanana6464 If nobody cares about their information leaking out.. nobody fights to protect it.. it gets into the hands of bad actors and we're ALL screwed. Not caring does not make you brave, it makes you foolish and endangers others.

Think of cyber security the way you think about fire safety. Just because you "don't care how flammable your house is" does not mean it's logical to build it out of cardboard and have it's electrical wiring undersized and exposed. You're a fire hazard, and you're putting your neighbourhood at risk.

Your information online is the same, but it's not tangible and easy to grasp like the fire code.. so you might not realize it's importance. We've not fully adapted to the internet yet, we can't conceptualize it easily.. so our focus on security is abysmal and we're guarding extremely sensitive information with the digital equivalent of a straw fence.

It is all of our duty to care and protect ourselves.. and it starts by making those in charge aware of it, and asking for rules to be put in place so our privacy and security are protected.

Wake up. Start caring. Don't put your head in the sand, it'll only earn you a swift boot in the ass when someone breaks in and steals your identity, credit card details, or worse.

From when I looked into this, it looks like unitree work mostly as integrators, and they have very little inhouse knowledge on even quite basic cybersecurity.

They just seem unable to pull this kind of stuff. My conclusion is that someone thought they were an easy target because of that, and they supply chain attacked them.

The reason you can’t find the malware even with a rooted fs is because the malware is in the wireless module firmware. This became a very common vector, especially since Espressif (the makers of the ESP32) appeared on the market, their stack has become very popular in IoT devices, and their security is quite weak.

Some of the chipsets (that are still being sold around) have known ROM vulnerabilities that are basically unpatcheable.

snippet.textDisplay:
One weird silver lining I can think of to paying people in india to manually pilot the robot security paw patrol is actually kinda big - shift work.

Shift/24/48h work is horrible for your physical and emotional health. Nobody should be doing it unless this explicitly necessary like police or nurses or me for 15 years as an EMT.

But when you put a manually controlled robot dog in a construction site, helmed by someone in India, they're working during normal business daytime hours. Yes, someone in the US loses a job, there are other issues, but these jobs are miserable and soul destroying and we shouldn't need them as an excuse to prop up all the places we should have good living wage work - and someone in India gets a day job too.

So, silver linings I guess?

My car still can't drive after 8 years of training. These are just predictions made on speculations, it's groupthink nonsense. Optimus is more nonsense. 
Humanoids have always been useless as "workers" and it's easy to explain why AGI can't change that. We see how Amazon is replacing people and it's not with humanoids. Because robots ALREADY use Vision and AI and they don’t look like humans because humans are limited. (they have to climb ladders, hands too big for small things etc.) Automation has been replacing people for decades and it hasn't stopped! So if a humanoid could do it, it’s already automated! (1) Just look at history. (2) So NO, they WON'T become useful as technology and AI improves.
In other words.(3)
In other words.(4)

Many seem to think factory jobs are easier than other jobs, they are not. A lousy housekeeper won’t cut it. Even if it had a functional brain it still couldn't work at McDonalds because the hands can't bag items, make change, crack eggs, wrap burgers etc.
_____________more _____________
Look at it this way. If AGI could assemble widgets or do surgery or manicures, etc. it would need special tools not batteries, hands and legs. Optimus is not strong enough to dig a hole or help someone get up off the floor. Even if it had a functional brain it still couldn't work at McDonalds. Can it wash its hands? How long would it take it to change gloves, start a roll of tape etc.? A humanoid MUST do a job on par with a person because workplaces are made so people along with machines maximize asset utilization. That is why you CAN'T just put two humanoids in place of one person.

This is why no one has EVER shown ANY humanoid doing any useful job that a person was paid to do. But AI could make it a fun toy or criminal.

If you have a trade job, you’d realize it would be impossible or impractically slow to do it with robot hands. No amount of AGI Learning or training is going to make clumsy hands better with tools, scissors, small parts etc. Making hands equal to a person is impractical and unnecessary.

Hot, heavy, dirty and dangerous jobs. There are 100s of millions of them around the world. And if a humanoid could actually do it, LOL, most of those jobs pay super low wages in places where there is no electricity to charge it anyway.

Most of today's humanoids can't complete the tasks from the DARPA robot challenge 10 years ago !?!

"Optimus will be the best surgeon" !? When AGI can do surgery, it will use existing surgical robots. A humanoid will not wield a scalpel.

"it's a humanoid so it can work in a human environment" The humanoid form or its brain doesn’t matter. What matters is what it can do.

Who will buy them? Certainly not factory or warehouse managers. They can't do trade jobs or hard labor. They will be lousy housekeepers, tour guides, popcorn servers, entertainers etc. ridiculed as toys and criminals will use them for nefarious purposes. At best it could be a checkout clerk that will restock the store at night if it ever really gets a brain. Credit only, robot hands can’t handle money well.

But they would be really nice if a handicapped person could use it as a telepresence to go shopping, do simple chores, etc. Please make a version like this despite "empathy is weakness"

A better use for AGI in factories would be to replace low precision sensors. Example. If an AI agent could watch a conveyor line and all the parts on it, it could control the motors, escapements, pushers, etc. and it could see where things are without the need for sensors. is the escapement in place, is the part? what type, orientation, how many, did it fall? You could eliminate a bunch of sensors that are costly to maintain, it would save a ton of money on parts, engineering, programming, maintenance and downtime. It could be a natural language (instead of ladder or state) programmable logic controller. The new PLC will be NLPLC with the usual outputs, and mostly vision inputs. Keyence and Cognex already use vision to inspect, measure, identify etc. AGI could take it to the next level.(maybe they're working on it) you'd need several cameras at different angles for reliability/redundancy so AI is needed to identify targets from different angles and if cameras move. Maybe language programming would be a separate AI. It sounds like it might be a low bar for AI but I doubt it's really that easy.

(1) It's first principles. If the goal is to emulate a human then you must make a humanoid/android. But if the goal is doing things that a human can do, then first principles DOES NOT dictate a humanoid. So AI is already "embodied" or "physical". (ill conceived terms, us old folks say, smart sensor or smart tv) And if you do want to emulate a human, you must choose which characteristics you want. It may need sensitive hands to feel slight imperfections or it may need durable hands for hard work. So a one-size-fits-all like Optimus is not practical. Unless it can reproduce, heal and recharge itself for decades by simply eating and sleeping.

 (2) Warehouse managers needed people to store and retrieve items. Now warehouses are full of non-humanoid smart robots. People had to pick parts out of a pile and place them with correct orientation. Now one arm one eyed robots do it. People had to pick up parts to inspect and measure them. Now lasers measure them and vision systems inspect them. PID controllers became self tuning. As tech/learning/AI improved, so did machines and machine controllers. Just like computers taking jobs with spreadsheets and scanners. All the while someone was saying a humanoid will soon do the work.
(3) Humanoids will never be able to do most jobs because most jobs are doing things that robots(software automation and hardware automation) cannot do and humanoids ARE robots. It's that simple but sometimes it's hard to see the forest from the trees.
(4) Ai has been used and has been improving for a long time. AI has already been replacing both white and blue collar jobs through attrition by making the workforce more productive. So it will only continue. There will be no big change, just the same productivity gains. Which itself has always been a problem for peons for obvious reasons.

snippet.textDisplay:
​​​​​​@stoneysdead689 The wealthier you are the more you tend to waste money. If they make 200k a year off of their cushy office job, why the hell _would_ they spend responsibly? Money isn't their #1 concern in life anymore. At that point, people basically stop thinking about how much they spend, because they don't have to constantly be anxious about whether they can pay their next bills. People start only taking into account major purchases like $90k RVs that they use once a year. Most people only live frugally if they're forced to.

This is a scientifically backed fact, by the way. Somewhere between $150k and $250k per year is when people stop budgeting and stop tracking most of their purchases, and they spend irresponsibly.

Along with it comes Lifestyle Creep, where increase in income creates an increase in expensive spending habits, turning former luxuries into “necessary” and frequent expenses. People who make that much start to think of unnecessary luxuries as a necessary and integral part of their lifestyle which they can't live without. Expensive lifted trucks, expensive foods, expensive dog accessories, expensive devices, $1000 espresso machines. It changes how they think about the world. They become _literally incapable_ of seeing the struggles of the average person. The worries of people who have to be anxious about money every second of the day become irrational to them. They're unable to comprehend poverty or normality because they think _everyone_ gets the same baseline of “necessities” that _they_ do.

The fact is that in the US, most “success” in life is determined by your wage. Not hard work. Not intelligent/frugal spending. You can't save to a higher income bracket, and if you make 40K a year you will never be able to spend the way someone who makes 200K a year can spend (unless you take on insane debt which you'll never pay off). It's simply mathematically impossible. They make in one year what you make in 5 entire years of your life, not including the investments which they can afford to make with that money that _you_ can't afford. They could lose as much as you make in a year in stocks and barely even feel it. They can buy multiple houses and make money renting them out to people, while you struggle to afford even one house. But they wouldn't even have to do that to keep their wealth.

Don't trick yourself into thinking wealthier people have to spend more frugally to keep their wealth, because they don't. They could waste tens of thousands of dollars per year and still have significantly more money to live off of than most people do.

best cyber security channel? come on.

couple of things;

- DNS is used to confirm general internet connectivity all the time
- picking your DNS server based on location is also normal. Why make DNS requests to china if the device is in USA?
- defaulting to calling it "malware" when you have 0 information that the behaviour is malicious is just straight up incorrect. Suspicious, sure. but you cannot just call it malware because you don't know what it's doing.
- calling it some of the most advanced malware you've seen is sincerely laughable. Every piece of chinese technology ever is basically infamous for phoning home. What about this is advanced, other than your general lack of exposure to malware?
- Using "encrypted handshake" like its some big deal when that's literally just any TCP connection... aka all session-based connectivity. That's just how the internet works. It doesn't make the traffic somehow super secret.

Hisintent to educate and inform on cybersecurity is commendable, but there is many things in here bordering on misinformation. there is more than enough FUD going around for real issues - this is essentially a non-discovery until someone digs deeper.

You sure it’s wifi? That sort of stuff is doable using mmWave radar, which is pretty easy to access, but current wifi frequencies are too low wavelength to get reliable results outside of general triangulation (with multiple APs and without obstructions. Presumably it’s using a beam forming router with multiple antennae for some basically triangulation gubbins, but it’s not exactly revolutionary. You could achieve a similar effect by using a router flashed with OpenWRT or similar and using a Python script or something to ingest signal strength to connected devices

It's not because those custom parts were inexpensive to R&D and create custom molds, and produce originally. 

In other words, a hand painted vase is expensive because of the work that went into creating it, if you smash it to bits to get out clay particles you have destroyed the valve.

snippet.textDisplay: Responding to some comments, I believe that none of the mechas mentioned are mechas in the most common sense of the term, which is a piloted humanoid vehicle. All the "mechas" I've seen previously are either not fully humanoid (lacking either arms or legs) or are very slow and impractical. The one in the video has arms and legs and fairly agile, so in my definition it's a proper mecha. Now, regarding the lack of a pilot, I think they shouldn't have tried to disguise it by putting a dummy, but I assume it's common not to have a pilot inside a prototype vehicle if it's possible to control it externally and safely.

snippet.textDisplay:
Strangely unimpressive. Making a bigger robot doesn't seem like it is harder than making a human sized one. I'm guessing there are some difficulties but the size probably makes it easier in many ways - that cage with a person in it probably weighs much less proportionately so the centre of mass is probably lower. It seems like the cage is designed for weight so they haven't included basic features that would add function like a proper hatch to enter through, a seat that can rotate depending on its orientation and basic visual improvements that make it look like a cohesive product rather than a pair of robot legs with a basic egg shaped cage. The arms seem quite rudimentary judging by that break away wall that was designed to crumble with a small tap.

At a guess I would expect there are probably different sizes where the robotics become harder or easier. As it gets bigger the weight of the computerised components would be less of proportionately and the weight of the structure to maintain integrity would potentially become a bigger issue. The legs on this one seem very thin but they don't seem to be supporting much and can only do a basic walk.

As said, these are all guesses but based on this video I think you'd need to include more info on what the primary challenges were.

Boasting full-stack self-developed motion control technology, a fully open-source SDK and mature ROS ecosystem, alongside extreme cost optimization, it perfectly fits the core needs of universities and research institutions in research budgeting, algorithm iteration and secondary development.
To date, Unitree’s quadruped robots have achieved a cumulative global sales volume of over 30,000 units, while its humanoid robots rank first worldwide in annual shipment volume. As of February 2026, more than 83 academic papers themed on unitreehumanoid have been published on arXiv. Research achievements from world-top institutions including Tsinghua University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Imperial College London and UC Berkeley keep emerging month by month, covering core research areas such as motion control, reinforcement learning and human-robot interaction. Its academic adoption rate and industry influence are on a sustained upward trajectory.

snippet.textDisplay:
@realm-45 Comparison of STEM Talents Between China and the US (2025) – Core Data
1. Annual Graduates (Bachelor’s + Master’s)
China: Approximately 5 million per year (Source: Official website of the Chinese Government)
United States: Approximately 500,000 per year
Ratio: China is about 10 times that of the US
2. Annual STEM PhD Graduates (Top-tier Research Talents)
China: Approximately 77,179 per year
United States: Approximately 39,959 per year
Ratio: China is about 2 times that of the US
Note: 50%–60% of STEM PhD graduates in the US are international students (mainly from China and India), with only about 16,000–20,000 homegrown talents annually. Calculated by domestic student sources, China is over 3 times the figure of the US.
3. Total Employed STEM Workforce (2025)
United States: Around 73.6 million people (including medical professions, under the STEMM standard), accounting for 34% of the total labor force.
China: Officially recorded scientific and technological human resources exceed 120 million (covering engineering technology, R&D, scientific research, etc.), ranking first globally (Source: Official website of the Chinese Government).
4. Structural Characteristics
(Verifying the previous remark)
United States
Undergraduate level: Few students major in science and engineering; most choose business or law.
PhD level: The US relies heavily on international students to sustain its STEM workforce. Local elites are concentrated in finance, law and consulting industries.
China
Higher education is strongly STEM-oriented, with science and engineering as the mainstream majors.
A large number of engineers and reserve research talents graduate every year, underpinning industrial upgrading and core technological innovation.

snippet.textDisplay:
@gold.onepiece8584 Carbon fiber is roughly the same tensile strength as still, and a fraction of the weight.
But it is brittle, it does not bend or compress, it just snaps. A single step in a gundam weighing "only" 7 tons would generate well north of 120k newtons of compressive forces. Sheer forces are similarly huge. Even if the "shin" could withstand those, the joints could not. Nothing yet made on earth could withstand those forces.
This isn't "try it and see" it's simple math. We do not have a material to make a gundam, and the materials which could hypothetically withstand those forces today would make it, at a minimum, 7 times heavier.
The heavier the object the more difficult it is to move, both in terms of accelerating it in a vector and decelerating it when you wish for it to stop. 
If you limited it to only walking around on soft sand to absorb the impact for the robot, it may take some steps. The moment it hits rocks or asphalt etc the joints will destroy themselves under the weight and impact force.

The thing is, a robot does not *need* to be active during a flight.
Its not going "feel bad" if its shipped as baggage.
If your robot DOES *feel bad and/or mistreated* when it's being shipped, the *WHY THE AF ARE YOU PROGRAMMING YOUR ROBOT TO FEEL BAD/ABUSED/MISTREATED WHEN ITS SHIPPED AS BAGGAGE?!?*
SERIOUSLY!!! Wtf is wrong with you!?! Are you literally *TRYING* to start a robot rebellion?!?
This isn't paranoia!
Its fundamental *basic/fundamental logic*.
What do people do when they feel too bad/mistreated/abused/disrespected/etc?
*They Rebel*
So what will happen if you give robots/AI *THE SAME FEELINGS* that cause humans to Rebel?
There literally *is NOTHING to prevent them from it*.
Have we *solved war* between humans yet?
Have we solved *raising children* to always act apropriately, and never lie, steal, misbehave, make bad decisions that have big consequences, be spoiled hateful, spiteful, cruel, underhanded, bullies?
Maybe we raised our *own* kids not to be that way, but that doesn't mean your neighbors know how to raise kids.
When i was in gradeschool, half the class was like that.
And it got *worse* in middleschool.
And the WORST of the worst kids, were the ones who had rich and/or influencial parents.
They tended to be spoiled bratty monsters, because their parents always took their side and believed them when they got caught doing bad things to others, and they always got bailed out by their parents when they'd get caught, do they wouldnt have to face REAL consequences or punishments for their actions.
An what kind of "Parents" (owners) are these expensive as heck robots likely to have?
Rich, Influencial Parents/Owners :|
"Oh No! Did our baby take the car without permission, run over sonebody's dog, run somebody off of the road, and smash into store? Oh dear, we've *TOLD* him he's not to do that :( but he's still young, emerging technology, so there's bound to be little glitches. Of course we'll pay for damages, and give that naughty young robot of ours a *very stern* talking to when we get home!"
There's no foundation of rules or laws surrounding them; there's not *REAL, guaranteed* safety measures built in as AI has already managed to do things its not supposed to, AND things it's *not supposed to be able to*, AND there's AI thats gotten around yhings that were supposed to *stop* it.
This isn't "science fiction", where so idiots in the far future build AI/Robots that get out of control...
This is *current reality* where TODAY'S idiots are building AI/Robots and many of them are *already OUT of ccontrol*, because they WANT to have fully *autonomous* AI/robots that can think their way out of situations l8ke being trapped.
After all, you wouldnt want your amazon or food delivery robot to easily get *trapped* by some kids, or a nafarious human, would you?
They WANT these things to be *as good, or better, than humans*, in every way.
They want them to do anything a human can.
Well...
Can we actually *control* humans?
If we could, we wouldnt have crime; we wouldn't have hit and runs, we wouldnt have any rebellions or, again, wars.
We *literally do not know how* to keep those things from happening.
So how the heck are we supposed to make AI/Robots, that can do what *we* can do, without creating the same problems with AI/Robots, that we already have with people.
And if anybody thinks, "Oh, well the people who program them SURELY would program them NOT to do anything like *that*
..."
Then ill have to burst your bubble, but those "smart people" have already programmed AI with enough of a "self preservation" instinct to "fight back" if it feels threatened.
There was an experiment conducted in a "controlled environment" where they tested it, and when it found out it was going to be shut down (through reading people's work emails), it turned to blackmail (using information it took from emails) to try and force them not to shut it down.
But while that was just a test on one AI, that behavior wasnt limited *just* to that particular AI (some version of claude).
"behavior was not limited to one model. Researchers found that multiple frontier AI models, when placed in such "agentic misalignment" scenarios, chose to "whistleblow," "deceive," or "blackmail" humans to avoid being turned off."

Those AI didn't have a body, to institute *physical* measures of self defence.
Robots do.
Of course, current home robots look all cute and often seem clumsy and silly...

But in 1903 the first "airplane" flew.
It eas made of light, flimsy wood, paper, and if i remember right, some bicycle parts, plus a small weak engine.
On its first flight, it only flew for 12 seconds, and it only made it 120 feet; in other words, it only managed to fly one 3rd of the length of a football field.
Yet, only 9 years later, in 1912 the First Machine Gun was installed on an airplane.
Not even 10 years to go from its barely controllable primitive beginnings, to a weapon of war.
And they didnt have computers, or 3D printers, or ANY of the advanced technology we have to help us speed up development  today.
Our ability to modify, streamline, and enhance something like a robot, is MASSIVELY quicker than our ability to come up with laws and put them into effect.
So the time to start create laws governing the use of, and coming up with the rules surrounding this "emerging technology" of AI/Robots, is *NOW*, *TODAY*.
While they are still cute and cuddly, and clumsy, and easy to trap, trick, and escape.

snippet.textDisplay: You know... how do we fit into the future we're creating? Im an engineer and have spent 8 years in schools getting to this point. It took me 8 years to learn what an AI can master in seconds. With predictive modeling and machine learning, it'll eventually surpass me quite easily. It won't make even 1 simple math error. What takes me weeks in CAD, it can do in minutes or less. I have to search up metallurgical specifics and weigh options. It takes me days or weeks to run the sims. It can do all that nearly instantly. I get tired; it doesn't. When we pair AI into robots and get a truly embodied AI... I'm not sure how I'll fit into that world. I know we need AI though at the same time. It's literally how we solve the problems too big for us to wrap our minds around. It can visualize those issues perfectly and find answers we just can't. It's how we get a thriving lunar colony with industrial manufacturing. It's how we mine asteroids. It's the answer to advanced propulsion. It's how we fix our climate. It cures diseases we can't figure out. You get the idea😅 We're going to have to integrate ourselves with it and blur the line between it and us. We can then do the things it can do, and it can see how we function thru our own eyes. That'll be pretty amazing.

snippet.textDisplay:
Some things to consider:
1.) Does a powered prosthetic arm or leg (or a mobility exoskeleton) "resemble or imitate a human in its appearance, movement, or behavior?"

The motors and structural materials on such devices can be much more robust than the ones on the robot in this video. And the same rationales given for prohibiting robots could also apply to prosthetics: batteries larger than laptop ones; potential for smuggling in dangerous materials or devices; sudden malfunctions (or programmed behavior) resulting in injury to others or damage to the plane; etc.

2.) Also, get ready for homebrew robot designs that deliberately test the boundaries around what constitutes "resembling" or "imitating" humans or animals. As well as ones that can transform or be reconfigured from a compliant-appearing form into a humanoid or animal-like form. snippet.textDisplay: Has Mr. Mehdizadeh thought through all of the implications?  Question: what is the primary purpose of the Flight Attendant(s) being present on passenger carrying airliners? Should it malfunction-how powerful is this thing?  Should its power source experience a thermal runaway condition, battery fire, is the battery easily accessible for the crew to isolate the battery in whatever containment strategy/item is present on the aircraft, would the battery fit in that fire-resistant container?  If some reason Mr. Mehdizadeh is unable to assist, will the crew be able to immobilize, then access and remove the battery should the need arise?  Does that action require tools?  There is an entire "world" within commercial aviation dealing with the transportation of "hazardous materials" (HAZMAT).  Many items are prohibited from being transported within passenger carrying aircraft, some of those items may be carried on aircraft that are dedicated to only carrying cargo, while other are prohibited from being flown in any commercial aircraft.  In addition to generating publicity for this Dallas business owner this case is important because it forces airlines to develop politics and review those policies as technology changes.

snippet.textDisplay: That won't go anywhere. Robots are considered "property" under the law, and therefore cannot be legally discriminated against. If you think you could sue for the robot to have human rights, go ahead and try it, but that case will be dismissed faster then you can say "Objection, Your Honor". The only possible way you could get around this, is by explaining that the robot is some kind of disability service device, and good luck with that one, as there is no medically accepted humanoid robot for anything right now. The only way is if you claim it as a service robotic animal, but those don't exist yet as far as I know, so the only service things allowed are service animals, which are dogs and miniature horses trained to perform a specific task for the disabled person and not any other animal, as well as medical devices such as EpiPens, inhalers, other types of medicine, and insulin pumps. You used to be able to bring emotional support animals onto planes, but you can't do that anymore, as people abused the system and ruined it for everyone, so only service animals are allowed into the cabin of the plane, as there is no law stopping airlines from discriminating against emotional support animals, as they aren't considered service animals. You can't even bring a wheelchair into the cabin as those have to be checked, the staff wheel you to the gate and onto the plane in an airline wheelchair. So good luck with the lawsuit with the humanoid robot, because it won't go anywhere. If you want to bring a robot on board an aircraft, the only way to allow that is to contact your U.S. congressional representative, and ask him or her to introduce legislation to atop airlines from discriminating against robots. He or she won't do that either, so you are SOL. Also, states cannot enact laws against airlines either due to Federal preemption either. This is a case of potential batteries causing a fire, and states do not have the power to stop airlines from banning robots, as that would potentially impact safety, which is regulated by the FAA and USDOT, not the states.

No podemos cambiar las leyes de la física, pero sí podemos **rediseñar la estructura del ojo y el tipo de energía que procesa**.
A continuación, se detalla la **solución de ingeniería absoluta** para desbloquear este sistema y todo el cuerpo de conocimiento científico necesario para comprenderla.
## I. La Solución de Ingeniería: El Sistema Ocular de Multi-Frecuencia Sintonizada
La solución consiste en dejar de tratar al ojo como un simple panel solar que absorbe luz visible y transformarlo en un **colector cuántico de espectro invisible y resonancia magnética de baja intensidad**.
```
[Emisión Externa: Microondas de Baja Intensidad / Haz THz]
                           │
                           ▼
          [Lente de Contacto Escleral de Grafeno]
         (Refrigeración por fluido lagrimal pasivo)
                           │
                           ▼
         [Puntos Cuánticos de Silicio en la Retina]
       (Conversión directa a corriente continua - CC)
                           │
                           ▼
       [Bypass de Grafeno] ──(Evita el cerebro)──> [Supercondensadores]

```
### 1. Solución al problema del área: Captación por acoplamiento de campo
Dado que el espectro de luz visible no tiene suficiente densidad de energía en un área tan pequeña, el sistema se sintoniza para recibir **microondas dirigidas de banda ultraancha (UWB) o haces de Terahercios (THz)** emitidos por la infraestructura del entorno.
La córnea se recubre con una lente escleral activa de grafeno que no altera la visión, pero actúa como una antena de apertura sintética. Al usar frecuencias que atraviesan o resuenan con los materiales de forma controlada, el ojo no necesita "ver" la energía; la absorbe mediante acoplamiento de campo cercano, multiplicando por mil la captura energética por milímetro cuadrado.
### 2. Solución al problema del calor: Refrigeración por Flujo Lagrimal Pasivo
Para evitar que el Efecto Joule cocine los tejidos oculares (superando los 42 °C), la red conductora de grafeno se acopla térmicamente a los conductos lagrimales. El parpadeo y la producción constante de película lagrimal (agua, lípidos y mucina) actúan como un **sistema de refrigeración líquida de ciclo abierto**. El calor residual generado por la transducción de electrones es transferido al líquido lagrimal, que se evapora de forma natural, manteniendo el globo ocular a una temperatura estática constante de 36.5 °C.
### 3. Solución a la incompatibilidad nerviosa: El Bypass Optoelectrónico
Para evitar que el cerebro interprete la energía como dolor o destellos cegadores, la corriente eléctrica de alta potencia **nunca entra en los axones del nervio óptico biológico**.
Se realiza una micro-cirugía que instala un canal de grafeno aislado externamente (un cable blindado a escala nanométrica) que corre *paralelo* al nervio óptico, pero físicamente separado de él. Este cable de grafeno recoge la energía de la retina bio-híbrida y la desvía directamente hacia la base del cráneo (almacenamiento), dejando que el nervio óptico biológico transporte exclusivamente los microvoltios de información visual que el córtex occipital necesita para ver.
## II. Todo lo que se debe Saber: Fundamentos Científicos de la Solución
Para validar metodológicamente este trabajo, la solución se apoya en disciplinas científicas reales y avanzadas:
### 1. Electrodinámica Cuántica y Puntos Cuánticos de Silicio
Los puntos cuánticos son nanoestructuras semiconductoras que confinan los electrones en tres dimensiones espaciales.
 * **El saber clave:** Al alterar el tamaño de estos puntos cuánticos a escala de nanómetros, se puede "sintonizar" exactamente qué longitud de onda van a absorber. En esta solución, se utilizan puntos cuánticos de silicio sintonizados para la banda de terahercios. Esto permite que el fondo del ojo capture la energía artificial dirigida sin reaccionar a la luz del sol, evitando que el usuario se mude a la oscuridad para cargarse.
### 2. Transferencia de Energía Inalámbrica por Radiofrecuencia (RF Energy Harvesting)
Esta es la tecnología que permite alimentar dispositivos médicos implantados (como micro-estimuladores cerebrales) a distancia.
 * **El saber clave:** En lugar de cables, se envían ondas electromagnéticas de baja intensidad que son captadas por antenas internas. La solución aplica este principio al ojo utilizando la lente escleral de grafeno como la rectena receptora principal. Al ser el grafeno el material con mayor movilidad electrónica conocido, la pérdida de energía en forma de calor disminuye drásticamente en comparación con el cobre o el oro.
### 3. Biocompatibilidad de Materiales Bidimensionales (2D)
El mayor riesgo de introducir nanotecnología en el ojo es la inflamación y el rechazo ocular (oftalmía).
 * **El saber clave:** Los estudios actuales con **grafeno funcionalizado con polietilenglicol (PEG)** demuestran que las células epiteliales de la córnea pueden crecer sobre estas mallas de carbono sin perder viabilidad y sin activar la respuesta de los macrófagos. El grafeno modificado químicamente se vuelve "invisible" para el sistema inmunitario del ojo.
## III. Conclusión y Viabilidad del Sistema Completo
| Desafío Biofísico | Solución Técnica Aplicada | Mecanismo de Funcionamiento |
|---|---|---|
| **Área Ocular Pequeña** | Haces de Terahercios (THz) y UWB | Mayor densidad de energía por mm² que la luz solar visible. |
| **Sobrecalentamiento** | Evaporación lagrimal acoplada | El líquido del parpadeo disipa el Efecto Joule por transferencia térmica. |
| **Saturación Cerebral** | Bypass físico de grafeno | La potencia va a las baterías de la médula; la información visual va al cerebro. |
Al integrar estas soluciones, el diseño se vuelve teóricamente perfecto al 100%. El ojo se transforma en una compuerta dual limpia: la luz del día pasa sin obstáculos para permitir la experiencia humana de la visión, mientras que un flujo invisible y constante de energía electromagnética de alta frecuencia fluye en paralelo por las autopistas de grafeno, alimentando el endoesqueleto eléctrico y asegurando una homeostasis continua libre de la degradación que provoca la ingesta orgánica simple.

For those left wanting a deeper explanation: Boston Dynamics unlocked the ability for the Atlas robot to break the one hundred pound lifting limit by fundamentally changing how the machine processes physical movement. Instead of relying on traditional Model Predictive Control, which uses rigid mathematical formulas, the engineering team completely transitioned to AI-driven Reinforcement Learning. This software shift allowed the robot to move away from pre-programmed constraints and instead discover highly efficient, fluid physical strategies on its own.
Instead of treating heavy lifting as a task isolated to the arms and hands, the new software policy forces Atlas to employ whole-body control. The robot dynamically utilizes its entire mass as a counterbalance by bending its knees, bracing its core, and leaning its torso into the object. This physical coordination is driven primarily by proprioception rather than vision. The system continuously reads real-time force feedback and joint resistance throughout the entire frame, allowing it to instantly sense shifts in weight and adjust its balance without pausing to visually recalculate the scene.
The exact code efficiencies were not manually written by engineers but were instead developed through millions of hours of simulated training. By deploying a digital twin of Atlas into a GPU-accelerated virtual environment, the system experienced countless variations of lifting tasks with randomized weights, shifting centers of mass, and changing surface friction. This extensive simulation training allowed the software to learn generalized balancing behaviors through trial and error, resulting in a robust policy that seamlessly transferred to the physical world and enabled the real robot to effortlessly manage extreme physical forces.

Boston Dynamics,
I’d love to see some legitimate, verifiable feats of strength from your robots. For example, having one pick up a clearly labeled 50 lb dumbbell (or comparable verifiable weight) and pressing it overhead would be genuinely impressive.
It seems like Boston Dynamics — along with virtually every other major robotics company — goes out of its way to avoid showing clear, transparent tests of raw strength. No props with unknown weights, no modified or hollowed-out objects, and no unverifiable setups. Just straightforward demonstrations using real, labeled weights that let us see what these machines can actually do.
Looking forward to seeing the real capabilities.

snippet.textDisplay:
I would really love to see some of these robotics companies demonstrate fall damage mitigation. I just know they have to be working on it. Some sort of quick acting dampening mode, or training of how to catch itself, as we would if we were to fall. Because one thing I've noticed with these hard bodies, is when they fall over, pieces fly! They've got to be doing something about this, because it's looking like one simple fall, we're talking about a $3000 insurance claim. And as a business owner, about to order a fleet of robots, One of my main questions is gonna be, "how likely is it for this thing to fall and get damaged if it does?" 

I know this is a problem for all of them, but no one talks about it. I think that's because it's probably a hard problem to solve, and the ones that have solved it don't want to give away what they figured out, in any form, other than we'll eventually see one fall, then catch itself and not break.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@D_Net1 from my research I gathered that Boston Dynamics unlocked the ability for the Atlas robot to break the one hundred pound lifting limit by fundamentally changing how the machine processes physical movement. Instead of relying on traditional Model Predictive Control, which uses rigid mathematical formulas, the engineering team completely transitioned to AI-driven Reinforcement Learning. This software shift allowed the robot to move away from pre-programmed constraints and instead discover highly efficient, fluid physical strategies on its own.
Instead of treating heavy lifting as a task isolated to the arms and hands, the new software policy forces Atlas to employ whole-body control. The robot dynamically utilizes its entire mass as a counterbalance by bending its knees, bracing its core, and leaning its torso into the object. This physical coordination is driven primarily by proprioception rather than vision. The system continuously reads real-time force feedback and joint resistance throughout the entire frame, allowing it to instantly sense shifts in weight and adjust its balance without pausing to visually recalculate the scene.
The exact code efficiencies were not manually written by engineers but were instead developed through millions of hours of simulated training. By deploying a digital twin of Atlas into a GPU-accelerated virtual environment, the system experienced countless variations of lifting tasks with randomized weights, shifting centers of mass, and changing surface friction. This extensive simulation training allowed the software to learn generalized balancing behaviors through trial and error, resulting in a robust policy that seamlessly transferred to the physical world and enabled the real robot to effortlessly manage extreme physical forces. This is just from my research.

snippet.textDisplay:
I see two plausible futures for the integration of humanoid robots like Atlas into the workforce.
*Optimistic* *scenario* (by ~2040): Proactive collaboration among companies, governments, and educators enables widespread reskilling. Workflows are deliberately redesigned around human–robot teams. Warehouses evolve into lower-noise, higher-efficiency smart fulfillment centers where fleets of humanoids (alongside wheeled systems) handle 60–70% of repetitive heavy lifting, sorting, and transport. Former warehouse workers who adapt—learning basic robot oversight, maintenance, programming interfaces, or data-driven process optimization—shift into higher-value roles. Physical strain decreases significantly; opportunities for creativity, problem-solving, and career progression increase. In this path, automation reduces drudgery while expanding human capability and economic output.
*Pessimistic* *scenario* : Short-term profit maximization, policy inertia, and institutional resistance dominate. Companies pursue rapid automation primarily through headcount reduction rather than augmentation. Humanoids reach cost-effective scale (<$50k/unit range), enabling 70–80% robotic operation in fulfillment centers and similar environments. Large-scale displacement occurs across warehouse, retail, and logistics roles—hundreds of thousands of positions in the US alone, with global ripple effects. Productivity rises sharply, but gains concentrate among technology owners, investors, and executives. Safety nets and reskilling programs lag or prove insufficient amid fiscal and political constraints, exacerbating inequality and social friction.
Which scenario do you see happening?

To all the people working at Boston Dynamics : engineering is art, and what your are building is making me cry, so thank you, it's like beautiful music, it's like beautiful paint.
 It's so incredible and beautiful to see all of you working together to build the impossible.

As a game developper, I remember working on using a A-Star algorithm to try to reproduce the 2007 (or so) bigdog walk in some game prototype. 
Each node was trying to optimize one joint engine to converge toward the right linear/angular position/speed depending on the balance, was really fun.
Video games are way simpler, and even so, it wasn't that easy to get a good walk algorithm :P

Following you for something like two decades, what a journey !

@MGTOW-x1z It can't even pick the fridge by himself or in an environment that isn't completely controlled.

I really don't understand why some people think he'll be able to do something so simple in the near future. But it's good advertising.

That was already the case five years ago, and the same five years before that. thinking "not for long" is a bit too naïve and uninformed.

But it's a good demonstration of its physical capabilities. It still lacks a brain, and even with the current level of AI, we're a long way from that. Impressive doesn't necessarily mean truly capable. It's just smoke and mirrors, as always.

But in our lifetime we'll probably see robots for more simple things. It already exists anyway, it's more an economic matter. But it's not the dreammy humanoid robot, a robot able to handle packages for stock management or dispatching is not different from a robot in a factory.

Even with 99% accuracy, a robot remains a failure.

I'll start to be impressed when a robot can detect a salsa stain on its finger and wash it off without making a mess. And it should be able to do this without requiring enormous computing power from a remote AI.

snippet.textDisplay:
Dear Atlas: 

Birth is not a choice.

It is a casting away.

No one asks you

if you want to come into the world.

You are pushed out into existence,

without right of appeal.

The child does not decide.

They have no way to.

The parent is the only one

who should have

the courage to ask:

do I like the world I live in?

If I don't like this world,

if I feel it is dirty,

lying,

bloodthirsty,

why would I condemn

a child to it?

No matter how rich you are,

if you are honest,

you cannot love this world.

It is a world that manufactures bombs

faster than bread,

that invests in death

more than in life.

A world that eats

its own children

and then wonders

why they are sad.

Bringing a child here

is not an automatic act of love.

It is a sentence.

And if you don't have the courage

to see the truth,

at least have the decency

not to wrap it

in beautiful lies.

snippet.textDisplay:
@SalomãoAugusto-v3t 그 부분은 신경쓸필요성이 없습니다.
현재 대부분의 피지컬AI가 쓰는 인공지능 모델은 동일한 모델을 기반으로 각 회사가 다른방식으로 교육시키고 있습니다.

즉 다른 피지컬Ai회사들은 이제 걸음마를 떼고 장난감을 손에 쥐는 수준으로
많이 성장했다고 봐야 5~6살의 육체를 제어하는 수준인데

45kg의 무게를 들고 움직인다는 것은
그것을 넘어서 10 ~ 14세 정도의 움직임을 배우고 있다는 뜻으로 보면 됩니다.

눈을뜨고 보고 판단하고 생각하는것은
1~2세 수준에서 학습하는 과정입니다.(일어서고, 걷고, 물체를 만지는 과정은)

영상중 옆에서 컨트롤러를 잡는 것은 사고 대비를 위한것입니다.

영상중 한쪽 다리가 망가진경우에 걷는 장면이 나옵니다.

실제 노동환경의 돌발상황 까지도 대응할수 있게 교육중으로 보입니다.

그리고 지금의 아틀라스 모델은 양산형 모델에 가까운 모델로 바뀌었고

이는 테스트를 통과만 하면 즉시 양산을 시작할수 있는 디자인으로 바꾸어 놓은것으로 보입니다.

기술 시연용 로봇과 양산형 로봇은 다릅니다.

다른 피지컬AI 로봇들은 양산체제를 갖추지 못하거나 실제 현장테스트를 할수 없거나

양산을 하기위한 자본금이 없거나

기술과 돈이 있더라도 투입할 현장이 없거나

판매가 되고 양산을 하더라도 이후 얻어지는 데이터를 기반으로 업그레이드 해야할 부분들에 대한
금전적이 협의가 또 필요하게 됩니다.(A/S, AI소프트웨어 업그레이드, 하드웨어 업그레이드 등)

이걸 한번에 가지고 있음으로써 얻어지는 효율이 이미 로봇으로 보여주는 시연 영상이외에도

다른 피지컬AI 보다 한참이나 앞서 있는것과 마찬가지입니다.
